In addition, HAS is currently developing guidelines on supporting the development of self-determination
and empowerment within social and medico-social facilities or services (ESSMS).

The principles established in 2012 – namely that ASD interventions should be early, comprehensive,
based on a coherent and coordinated care pathway, and grounded in educational, behavioural and
developmental approaches (Grade B in 2012) – remained valid in 2025.

Given the limited evidence available in the literature, further research is required, particularly in clinical,
epidemiological and interventional fields.

From an epidemiological perspective, it is reiterated that there is no evidence of a link between ASD
and:

‒  vaccination (including measles, mumps and rubella);

‒  paracetamol use during pregnancy;

‒  screen overexposure, although this does not preclude their use.

Substantial efforts to scale up professional training (across the healthcare, social care, and health and
medico-social sectors), and to raise awareness in all areas of life (education, training, leisure, culture,
sport, employment, housing, etc.) are essential in order to improve intervention, action and support.

The steering group chose, by common agreement, to refer to the children and adolescents con-
cerned as “autistic children” or “autistic adolescents”.

The expression “Autism Spectrum Disorder” (ASD) is used when referring to the condition it-
self.

Unless the grade of the guideline is specified, all of the following recommendations are based on expert
consensus.  They  have  been  developed  on  the  basis  of  scientific  evidence,  which  includes
bibliographical references and discussions during meetings of the steering and rating groups.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

14

Recommendations

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

15

1.  Assessment of functioning

Key message

The  assessment  of  functioning  required  for  monitoring  autistic  children  and  adolescents  and  for
defining  their  personalised  intervention  plan  is  multidimensional,  multidisciplinary,  regular,  and
based on observations carried out and shared by parents and professionals.

In 2026, diagnostic assessment remains the first stage of therapeutic interventions.

Assessments  of  the  child’s/adolescent’s  development  and  health  status  are  intended  to  define  and
adjust  the  interventions  proposed  within  the  framework  of  a  personalised  intervention  plan,  and  to
ensure the consistency of that plan in light of updated knowledge [GPG 2012].

All assessments are centred on the child/adolescent. They take account of their unique characteristics
as well as those of their family and are conducted in close collaboration with them. All information must
be communicated to them both orally and in writing, in an accessible manner. The objectives and the
assessment tools used are explained to them [GPG 2012].

Before initiating this process, the guidelines [GPG 2012] recommend:

‒  organising a discussion with the child/adolescent, adapted to their communication abilities, and
with  their  parents,  in  order  to  understand  their  expectations  and  their  level  of  satisfaction
regarding the previously implemented or planned intervention plan;

‒  ensuring  that  the  initial  assessment  has  been  carried  out  in  accordance  with  current
recommendations and, where necessary, undertaking any examinations that have not yet been
completed;10

‒

requesting, with the family’s consent and in accordance with professional ethical standards, the
transfer  of  assessments  previously  carried  out  in  the  same  domains  by  another  team  or
professional.

The  implementation  of  interventions  may  begin  even  before  all  initial  assessments  have  been
completed, as soon as a developmental disorder is observed [GPG 2012].

The diagnostic process must be immediately linked to the implementation of interventions and requires
coordination between the diagnostic teams and the intervention teams [GPG 2012].

1.1.  Procedures for carrying out the functional assessment as part of

the child/adolescent’s follow-up

1.1.1.  A multidisciplinary assessment

Updating  the  personalised  plan  for  coordinated  educational  and  therapeutic  interventions  means
monitoring the child’s or adolescent’s developmental progress in their various areas of development.
For this reason, the assessment is multidisciplinary and, for all autistic children and/or adolescents,
draws on medical, psychological, paramedical and educational expertise [GPG 2012].

10 Cf. Autism Spectrum Disorder: Warning Signs, Identification, Diagnosis and Assessment in Children and Adolescents – HAS
2018.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

16

This multidisciplinary assessment, carried out by the usual team of practitioners, is recommended for
the  implementation  of  educational  and  therapeutic  interventions  (definition  or  updating  of  the
personalised intervention plan) [GPG 2012].

1.1.2.  A regular assessment

To adapt the personalised intervention plan, it is recommended that an assessment be carried out by
experienced professionals trained in assessing the various domains of development at least annually
for  every  autistic  child  or  adolescent.    This  assessment  is  systematically followed  by  a  case  review
meeting [GPG 2012].

1.1.3.  An assessment based on functional evaluation and the sharing of

observations

Any assessment aimed at monitoring the development of an autistic child or adolescent systematically
includes a physical/somatic examination, structured clinical observations, and informal observations of
the  child’s/adolescent’s  functioning  and  participation,  conducted  continuously  by  parents  and
professionals  during  the  proposed  interventions.  It  also  takes  account  of  assessments  carried  out
within  the  framework  of  the  personalised  education  plan  by  teaching  teams,  as  well  as  reviews
conducted during meetings of schooling monitoring teams led by the designated coordinating teacher
[GPG 2012].

The  structured  clinical  observations  required  to  update  the  personalised  plan  are  functional
assessments that are straightforward to implement and enable a description of the child’s/adolescent’s
functioning,  participation  and  emerging  abilities.  Their  frequency  must  be  at  least  annual  for  every
autistic  child  or  adolescent,    and  may  be  more  frequent  in  certain  domains  [GPG  2012].  The  main
assessment tools for children and adolescents are presented in Table 3, Table 4, Table 5, Table 6,
Table 7 (cf. GPG 2018).

However,  annual  structured  clinical  observations  alone  are  insufficient  to  adjust  the  functional
objectives of the interventions, to monitor their effectiveness for a given child/adolescent, and to ensure
the generalisation of the acquired skills. They must therefore be complemented by continuous informal
observation  of  the  child’s/adolescent’s  functioning  and  participation  across  their  different  living
environments  and  during  the  interventions  delivered  by  professionals  [GPG  2012].  The  tools
recommended for structuring clinical observations are presented in Table 8 and Table 9 [GPG 2012].

It is recommended that this informal observation be discussed regularly with the family and, where the
family agrees, shared between professionals. The sharing of observations between professionals may
take  different  forms:  team  meetings,  face-to-face  or  telephone  conversations,  written  records  or
session reports made available to other professionals (shared or consultable files, in compliance with
the ethical standards of each profession) [GPG 2012].

The  sharing  of  observations  between  professionals  is  organised  as  follows:  regular  formalised
reporting, case review meetings, and supervision by an experienced professional (preferably monthly
and at least quarterly). These frequencies should take account of the needs of the professional team
and of the autistic children or adolescents concerned.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

17

1.2.  Domains requiring regular monitoring for all autistic

children/adolescents

The  heterogeneity  of  clinical  profiles  and  developmental  trajectories  of  autistic  children  and
adolescents  requires  regular  assessment,  at  least  annually,  carried  out  by  the  intervention  team,
covering  all  the  domains  listed  in  Table  1  and  providing  a  synthesis  within  an  overall  view  of  the
child’s/adolescent’s development [GPG 2012].

Table 1. Domains requiring regular assessment

ICF*

Domains

Functioning

communication and language

social interactions or socialisation

cognitive functioning

sensory and motor functioning

emotions and behaviour

somatic health

Activities

independence in daily activities

and participation

learning, particularly academic and pre-vocational

Environmental factors

* ICF: International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health

The  assessments  include  evaluation  of  the  child’s/adolescent’s  functioning  and  development  by
domain,  together  with  continuous  observation  to  monitor  the  effectiveness  of  interventions  for  that
individual [GPG 2012] (cf. Table 3, Table 4, Table 5, Table 6, Table 7).

1.3.  Components of the personalised intervention plan

The  child’s/adolescent’s  plan  comprises  essential  and  interrelated  components:  educational,
pedagogical  and  therapeutic.  These  different  components  should  be  adapted  to  suit  to  each
child/adolescent, their strengths, needs and developmental trajectory [GPG 2012].

The personalised plan should therefore specify [GPG 2012]:

‒

‒

‒

the functional objectives to be achieved in each of the targeted domains following assessment;

the means proposed (types of activities, techniques, etc.) to achieve these objectives;

the  professionals  responsible  for  implementation  (in  the  educational,  pedagogical  and
therapeutic sectors);

‒

the timelines for reviewing these objectives.

Each professional contributing to the implementation of the personalised plan defines concrete criteria
for the interventions they carry out, which will enable them to assess whether the objectives have been
achieved and are operational, and, where necessary, to adjust the intervention objectives if they prove
too ambitious or insufficiently ambitious for the child/adolescent [GPG 2012].

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

18

Although specific domains of intervention are identified, they are intrinsically interlinked, interactive and
complementary.  The interventions must therefore be implemented in a coherent manner [GPG 2012].

Assessment generally leads to the identification of needs requiring the involvement of professionals
from  different  disciplines,  and  sometimes  from  different  organisations  or  modes  of  practice.  The
expected contribution of each participant, as well as the coordination arrangements, must be specified
in the personalised coordinated intervention plan [GPG 2012].

Meeting these children’s and adolescents’ needs requires consultation among stakeholders (primarily
the parents, with the involvement of the autistic child or adolescent) in order to develop a shared vision
and to ensure that the services and interventions offered are as consistent and timely as possible [GPG
2012].

Particular  attention  should  be  paid  to  this  need  for  early  and  coherent  intervention  when  the
involvement  of  professionals  required  to  implement  coordinated  interventions  for  the  child  or
adolescent involves a referral decision by the Commission for the Rights and Autonomy of People with
Disabilities (CDAPH) and the definition of a personalised compensation plan [GPG 2012].

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

19

2.  Family support and training, taking

account of their experiential expertise

Key message

Support and training for parents are essential and must take account of their experiential expertise.
This  encompasses  a  range  of  approaches,  including  guidance,  psycho-education,  therapeutic
education,  parent support groups, mutual aid and social support  groups, peer-led support for the
families of people concerned, and respite schemes.

The combination of family support and training with interventions proposed for the child is a key factor
in creating an environment that is more conducive to the development of autistic children and to im-
proving families’ quality of life.

It is recommended that careful consideration be given to how parents and their children are received
and  supported.  These  arrangements  should  be  adapted  to  the  age  of  the  child  or  adolescent  and
incorporated, in the form of protocols, into the institutional or service plan [GPG 2012].

Each family develops its own modes of interaction. It is therefore important to consider the diversity
and complexity of family situations (cultural, social and economic), to clarify, where necessary, issues
relating  to  parental  responsibility 11  separated  parents,  blended  families,  single  parents,  siblings,
guardians, etc.), and to acknowledge any legal decisions or orders concerning the child/adolescent.
Unless otherwise determined by a court decision, it is recommended to promote and maintain contact
with both parents [GPG 2012].

It  is  recommended  that  the  personalised  intervention  plan  be  co-constructed  by  parents  and
professionals,  in  order  to  obtain  shared  agreement  among  all  stakeholders  (objectives,  proposed
means, implementation arrangements) [GPG 2012].

Efforts  should  be  made  to  ensure  that  parents  and  their  child  understand  the  objectives  of  the
interventions,  the  means  implemented  (roles  of  each  participant,  strategies  used,  etc.),  and  that
parental consent is obtained, in accordance with the principles set out in the Law of 4 March 2002 on
patients’  rights  and  the quality  of  the  healthcare  system,  and  the  Law  of  2  January  2002 reforming
social welfare and socio-medical action [GPG 2012].

It is recommended to encourage parents to speak freely, listen to their needs and offer them various
forms of support [GPG 2012].

Particular  attention  should  also  be  paid  to  signs  of  distress  and  requests  for  support  expressed  by
siblings, and a variety of support options should be offered: individual psychological support, “parents-
children-siblings” themed groups, discussion groups, organisation of joint activities with siblings, etc.
These options should not be imposed [GPG 2012].

Parents are advised to be particularly cautious regarding interventions presented by professionals or
organisations either as a means of completely eliminating the symptoms of ASD or even completely

11 Throughout this guideline, reference is made to situations in which parental responsibility is exercised jointly by the child’s father
and mother (Article 371-1 of the French Civil Code). In certain situations, however, the arrangements for joint parental responsibil-
ity may be modified, particularly in cases of parental separation or of a change in residence of one parent. In other cases, parental
responsibility may be delegated by the parents, or partially or wholly withdrawn by a judge. A guardian may then be appointed; this
also applies in the event of the parents’ death, or where the person concerned has reached the age of majority, which marks the
end of parental responsibility but places them under a guardianship order.  Depending on the circumstances, it may therefore be
appropriate to inform and involve the holders of parental authority or the guardians of the minor or the protected adult.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

20

curing their child, or as a method requiring exclusive use of that support, as discontinuing interventions
may pose a risk or lead to a loss of opportunities for the individual (e.g. discontinuation of treatments
for associated conditions12) [GPG 2012].

In  light  of  evidence  of  effectiveness  and  professional  experience,  parental  involvement  in
comprehensive  interventions  is  recommended  to  ensure  consistency  in  interactions  with  the  child
(Grade B) [GPG 2012].

2.1.  Impact on parents’ quality of life

Support for parents has a positive impact on their quality of life. It reduces parental stress, enhances
their sense of competence, and improves overall family dynamics.

Parental  support  includes  parental  guidance,  psychoeducation,  parenting  skills  training,  therapeutic
patient education, parent support groups, mutual aid and social support groups, caregiver training, and
various  respite  services  (for  example,  short-term  care,  in-home  respite  support,  or  respite  holiday
programmes).

Parents of autistic children and adolescents are included within caregiver support policies. As such,
they benefit from specific information (notably through autism resource centres, departmental disability
centres, coordination and referral platforms, family associations, etc.).

It is recommended to:

‒  offer  parental  guidance  (for  example,  see  Guidance  on

Intellectual  Disability  and
Neurodevelopmental Disorders, PACT and Jasper) to parents as soon as autism is suspected;

‒  provide specific support to help parents manage the key post-diagnostic stage, notably access

to information and rights;

‒  actively offer families support tailored to their needs and expectations (for example, caregiver
training provided by autism resource centres, and free information resources and educational
materials provided by the national autism network); to take parental stress into account in order
to prevent the risk of burnout;

‒  help parents better understand the functioning of their autistic child, regardless of age;

‒  explain the interventions to be implemented in collaboration with professionals;

‒  value  and  strengthen  parents’  educational  skills  so  that  they  can  be  adapted  to  their  child’s

specific needs in daily life;

‒  provide  parents  with  practical  tools  through  educational  programmes  and  hands-on  training,

enabling them to acquire the knowledge needed to support their child;

‒  offer parents social, emotional, informational and material support, and to identify and address

families’ respite needs;

‒  systematically  include  parental  support  as  an  essential  component  of  the  child’s  pathway,

ensuring the continuity and coherence of support;

‒

inform families about local services and resources (in particular via autism resource centres,
departmental  disability  centres,  coordination  and  referral  platforms  for  neurodevelopmental
disorders, family associations, mutual aid groups, independent practitioners, etc.);

‒

train professionals in reciprocal knowledge and skill sharing techniques with parents.

la vigilance des personnes et des familles sur les risques de dérives liées à certaines pratiques” (“Raising awareness among indivi-
duals and families of the risks associated with certain practices”).

21

2.2.  Impact on their children’s quality of life

Parental support promotes consistency in interventions, the generalisation of learning in everyday life,
and contextual adaptations, while enabling the prevention and management of challenging behaviours.
It is recommended to:

‒

involve parents in assessments of functioning and to explain their role in selecting interventions
in the cognitive, communication, sensory, motor and emotional domains;

‒

inform, train and support parents with regard to:



the monitoring of their child’s health (e.g. oral health, sleep, bowel function);

  environmental adaptations (particularly sensory and temporal structuring);

  strategies for preventing and managing challenging behaviours.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

22

3.  Interventions

Key messages

The recommended comprehensive interventions are developmental and behavioural in nature. They
should begin as early as possible – as soon as the first diagnostic concerns are raised – and continue
throughout childhood and adolescence, with increased vigilance during the transition to adulthood.

The  interventions  concern  multiple  functional  domains,  such  as  independence  in  daily  living,
communication, social skills, sensory processing and motor skills.

All  intervention  plans  systematically  include  a  personalised  component  aimed  at  improving
communication in the autistic child or adolescent.  They may be implemented without preconditions.
Where  indicated,  Augmentative  and  Alternative Communication  (AAC)  –  a  key  component  of the
overall plan – should be introduced from the earliest stages of support.

Consideration  should  be  given  to  adapting  the  environments  in  which  autistic  children  and
adolescents  live  (physical  spaces, temporal  organisation,  information)  in  order  to  align  them  with
their individual needs.

Technical  aids  can  be  used  to  facilitate  the  remote  monitoring  of  specialist  interventions.  These
include tele-expertise and digital tools.

3.1.  Comprehensive developmental and behavioural interventions

Key principles:

‒

‒

‒

respect the preferences of parents and autistic children or adolescents, family priorities, and
the principles of respectful care;

take account of the specific characteristics of each child or adolescent and their family;

include objectives relating to the generalisation of learning in different contexts of daily life,
so that the children or adolescents can use their skills in a variety of situations;

‒  combine group-based and individual sessions.

Behavioural  and  developmental  interventions  are  grounded  in  several  theoretical  frameworks,
including learning theory [GPG 2012].

The aims of these interventions [GPG 2012] are to:

‒  provide the children and their families with a secure relational environment;

‒  promote  the  development  of  the  children/adolescents  in  functional  domains  (communication
and  language,  social  interaction,  sensory  and  motor  functioning,  cognitive,  emotional  and
affective  development),  as  well  as  their  social  and  educational  participation,  autonomy,
independence, learning and adaptive skills;

‒

reduce environmental barriers that exacerbate their disability;

‒  contribute to their well-being and personal fulfilment.

Accordingly, it is recommended [GPG 2012] to:

‒  define  and  prioritise  the  proposed  interventions  based  on  the  results  of  assessments  in  the

different domains of functioning and social participation of the children/adolescents;

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

23

‒  monitor and assess the proposed interventions on the basis of continuous assessment of the

children’s/adolescents’ development, involving both these individuals and their parents;

‒  adapt the interventions according to the child’s/adolescent’s age and developmental level.

Regardless  of  their  age,  the  intensity  and  content  of  interventions  must  be  determined  in  line  with
ethical considerations aimed at limiting the risks of both under-stimulation and over-stimulation [GPG
2012].

If no clear progress is observed after several months, the choice of approaches, their implementation,
and the objectives, duration or frequency of interventions should be reviewed and adjusted, following
discussions between the family and professionals, and, if necessary, after consultation with a specialist
team or an autism resource centre [GPG 2012].

3.1.1.  Early interventions (Table 2)

It  is  recommended  to  initiate  early  intervention  in  autism  upon  the  appearance  of  the  first  warning
signs, 13 without  awaiting  confirmation  of  the  diagnosis,  and  to  continue  the  intervention  once  the
diagnosis has been confirmed (cf. Diagnostic GPG, HAS 2018).

Early  intervention  encompasses  any  developmental  and  behavioural  intervention  covering  physical,
sensory, motor, socio-emotional, cognitive and communication domains.

It includes direct interventions with the infant or child, the provision of parental guidance and support
for  early  childhood  professionals  and  settings,  such  as  early  years  childcare  services,  childminders
and nursery schools).

In the framework of early intervention, it is recommended to offer infants and children with a confirmed
risk  or  diagnosis  of  ASD  at  least  10  hours  per  week  of  interventions  delivered  by  professionals
specifically  trained  in  developmental  and  behavioural  approaches  and  in  the  provision  of  parental
guidance. In addition to these 10 hours per week, it is recommended to offer parent-mediated activities
at home in addition to interventions delivered by early childhood and educational professionals.

For autistic children under six years of age, priority should be given to early interventions supported by
evidence  of  effectiveness  capable  of  influencing  developmental  trajectories.  These  include  early
behavioural  and/or  developmental  interventions  such  as  Early  Intensive  Behavioural  Intervention
(EIBI), naturalistic developmental behavioural interventions (NDBI), developmental interventions, and
parent-mediated  interventions  (PMI)  (see  the  detailed  list  of  recommended  comprehensive  early
interventions in Table 2 below). Table 10 describes a broader range of comprehensive interventions.

Early intervention should actively support and organise parental involvement in responses to children’s
needs, as jointly assessed, in all aspects of daily life.

In  collaboration  with  parents,  it  is  recommended  to  evaluate,  on  a  regular  basis,  the  effects  of
interventions  on  the  child’s  development,  as  well as  their  acceptability  for  both the  parents  and  the
child.

It is also recommended to promote the inclusion of autistic infants and young children in mainstream
group settings (early years provision and nursery school).

3.1.2.  Interventions during childhood and adolescence

It is recommended to offer autistic children and adolescents a personalised intervention programme
based on a graduated, coordinated and coherent pathway.

This  programme  should be  tailored  according  to the results  of  a comprehensive  assessment  of the
children's or adolescents’ development and functioning in all domains (notably the adaptive, cognitive,
emotional,  communication,  motor  and  sensory  domains),  in  line  with  the  list  of  recommended
assessments, as well as their chronological age and interests.

The programme includes structured interventions combined with parent-mediated periods during daily
life.

It is recommended to provide training for parents of autistic children and adolescents through psycho-
education programmes, parenting skills training and/or therapeutic education in order to involve them
actively in day-to-day support.

Peer support should be encouraged (for example, family peer support or peer support between children
or adolescents).

It is recommended to ensure the consistency of interventions (educational, rehabilitative, pedagogical,
clinical  and  social)  by  involving  families,  and  to  promote  the  generalisation  of  the  children’s  or
adolescents’ skills throughout all of their living environments.

  It is recommended to implement developmental and behavioural interventions:

‒  prioritise interventions supported by the highest level of evidence of effectiveness, particularly

for improving social communication, cognitive abilities and adaptive behaviour;

‒  offer autistic children and adolescents aged 6 to 19 years opportunities to participate in social
skills  training  groups,  which  have  proven  to  be  effective  in  improving  functioning  in  autistic
children and adolescents without intellectual disability (Grade B);

‒

‒

for autistic children aged 6 to 12 years, begin with cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), which
has shown significant effects on improving social communication (Grade C);

for children aged 6 to 12 years, include parent-mediated behavioural interventions to reduce
challenging behaviours (Grade B).

  It is recommended to assess progress in each domain on a regular basis:

‒

‒

regardless of the intervention programme (Table 3), use standardised tools and/or scales for
monitoring, in order to adjust interventions according to personalised assessments of needs;

reassess the relevance of interventions in the absence of progress or in the event of symptom
worsening, using a framework for identifying potential causes;

‒  carry  out  standardised  functional  assessments  of  the  autistic  child  or  adolescent  at  least

annually, and more frequently during early childhood and at key transition stages;

‒

involve parents in these ongoing assessments in order to strengthen their role in any necessary
adjustments.

3.1.3.  Non-recommended interventions

It is incumbent upon the French National Authority for Health (HAS) to recommend only approaches
supported by robust scientific data and to avoid methods that are not supported either by evidence or
by consensus among experts appointed to develop a recommendation. However, some methods and

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

26

approaches assessed by HAS according to the principles set out in the methodological guide for clinical
practice guidelines have either not been the subject of scientific studies or are supported by studies
with insufficient quantitative and/or qualitative evidence, in contrast to the substantial body of data in
the literature supporting other therapeutic approaches recommended by the HAS. Under these condi-
tions, the following methods and approaches are not recommended:

  due to an absence of studies:

  Doman-Delacato,

  Feuerstein,

  Padovan method or neurofunctional reorganisation;



facilitated communication and related methods, such as the Rapid Prompting Method;

  Saccade®;

  due to an insufficient level of evidence:

  primitive reflex integration;

  Son-Rise®;

  3i;

  neurofeedback;

  psychoanalysis and other interventions based on psychoanalytic approaches;

  Snoezelen;

  due to studies demonstrating a lack of effect:

  “auditory integration” practices, including the Tomatis method (Grade B) [GPG 2012];

  “packing.”

3.2.  Interventions by functional domain

It is important to note that activities targeting a specific domain do not necessarily generalise to other
domains. Professionals must therefore ensure that skills acquired in a specific context are generalised
to other contexts [GPG 2012].

It is also recommended to involve families and other professionals working with the child/adolescent in
order to facilitate this generalisation [GPG 2012].

3.2.1.  Domain of independence in activities of daily living

For every child or young person with autism, the personalised plan must include functional objectives
relating to independence in activities of daily living (dressing, personal hygiene, shopping, household
chores,  meals,  transport,  etc.),  with  a  view  to  promoting  the  development  of  personal  and  social
independence  through  specific  learning  during  rehabilitation  sessions (e.g.  occupational  therapy) or
educational activities, followed by training in real-life situations at home, at school, at work, at leisure
or holiday destinations, and in public places in general that the child or adolescent is likely to visit [GPG
2012].

For  each  of  the  domains  considered  below,  it  is  essential  to  build  on  the  interests  and  individual
strengths of the autistic child or adolescent, as identified by professionals and families, in order to use
them to foster learning and socialisation.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

27

3.2.2.  Communication interventions

The communication and language domain is a key area in which assessment by the intervention team
is recommended for all autistic children and adolescents throughout their care and support pathway
[GPG 2012].

At a minimum, this assessment includes monitoring the development [GPG 2012] of:

‒  non-verbal communication (joint attention, imitation, frequency of communication initiation, turn-
taking, use of visual supports such as pictograms, etc.), even before the development of spoken
language;

‒

the receptive and expressive components of the different dimensions of language: phonological,
lexical, semantic, syntactic and pragmatic.

Language development should be monitored in spoken language (or sign language where appropriate)
and, from the age of 6, in both spoken and written language, even where the development of spoken
language  is  limited.  It  should  also  specify  whether  the  child  uses  an  alternative  or  augmentative
communication system [GPG 2012].

The  early  provision,  within  any  personalised  plan,  of  Augmentative  and  Alternative  Communication
(AAC) tools is recommended, paying attention to ensuring the generalisation of their use throughout
the  child’s/adolescent’s different  environments  (home,  school  and/or specialised  settings,  and  other
social contexts) (Grade C). Parents need to be trained in the use of these tools in order to support this
generalisation. When a child aged 6 years or older does not speak, written language teaching should
not be excluded [GPG 2012].

Autistic  children  and  adolescents,  with  or  without  intellectual  development  disorder,  always  exhibit
communication difficulties, whether or not these are associated with language disorders.

All intervention plans must include a personalised communication component, regardless of the child’s
or adolescent’s level of communication.

It is recommended that this component:

‒  be  based  on  a  comprehensive  assessment  of  all  aspects  of  the  child’s  or  adolescent’s
functioning,  as  well  as  environmental  facilitators  and  barriers;  any  trained  professional  may
contribute to the assessment of communicative functioning, in collaboration with parents;

‒  address  both  receptive  and  expressive  communication,  enabling  the  child  or  adolescent  to

understand, adapt to situations, and express agreement, refusal, opinions and consent;

‒

involve  and  support  the  family  as  a  central  stakeholder  in  the  communication  plan,  which
requires appropriate information and training for parents;

‒  be  generalised  throughout  the  individual’s  environments  and  to  his  or  her  communication

partners;

‒  be  based  on  the  child’s  or  adolescent’s  interests,  drawing  on  the  expertise  of  those  around

them;

‒

incorporate behavioural and developmental strategies to encourage communication initiatives
by the autistic child or adolescent.

A speech and language therapy assessment of communication and language, including their pragmatic
aspects, is recommended as part of both the diagnostic and functional assessment of the autistic child
or adolescent.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

28

In  the  presence  of  difficulties  in  communication,  oral  and  written  language,  writing,  mathematical
cognition,  orofacial  myofunctional  disorders,  feeding  and  swallowing,  or  dysfunctional  swallowing
disorders,  it  is  recommended  to  refer  to  speech  and  language  therapy  and  associated  disciplines
(psychomotor therapy, psychology, occupational therapy).

As  communication  difficulties  (expressive  and  receptive)  are  a  major  risk  factor  for  challenging
behaviours, speech and language assessment should be included in the functional assessment where
such behaviours are present.

Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC)

A personalised communication plan may be implemented without preconditions for autistic children or
adolescents,  including  for  the  introduction  of  Augmentative  and  Alternative  Communication  (AAC),
which constitutes a core component of the overall intervention plan.

It is recommended to:

‒

individualise the AAC plan based on collaboration with families and all professionals, and on an
evolving and coordinated functional assessment;

‒  use a range of tools and multimodal supports, which may be visual, gestural, with or without
technology,  prioritising those that promote the development of communication by the autistic
child or adolescent;

‒  promote  the  involvement  of  communication  partners,  who  play  a  key  role  in  modelling,
understanding, supporting and guiding the autistic child’s or adolescent’s communication while
respecting their individual characteristics;

‒  adapt  modelling  to  the  sensory  and  social  communication  profile  of  the  autistic  child  or

adolescent;

‒

individualise and adjust communication approaches and tools to meet their current and future
needs;

‒  where possible, use digital supports for Augmentative and Alternative Communication, such as

tablets;

‒  ensure  that  the  communication  plan  is  supervised  by  a  healthcare  or  support  professional
specifically trained in AAC, in partnership with the autistic child or adolescent, their family, and
other  professionals,  in  order  to  ensure  consistency  and  generalisation  throughout  all  living
environments.

3.2.3.  Interventions focused on social skills

The  social  interaction  domain  is  a  key  area  in  which  assessment  by  the  intervention  team  is
recommended,  for  all  autistic  children  and  adolescents  throughout  their  care  and  support  pathway
[GPG 2012].

At a minimum, this functional assessment includes monitoring the development [GPG 2012] of:

‒  play skills (e.g. imitation, turn-taking, initiating, maintaining and ending play interactions);

‒  social skills and interactions in different situations (establishing and maintaining relationships
with family  members,  peers,  professionals,  unfamiliar  individuals  and,  subsequently,  intimate
relationships);

‒  social skills and interactions in different settings (initiating, maintaining and ending interactions
at home, in childcare settings, at school, in healthcare and medico-social institutions, private
practice, etc.).

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

29

It is recommended to:

‒  use social skills training groups, as early as possible and at least from the age of 6, in order to

improve social and friendship skills in autistic children and adolescents;

‒  offer these interventions individually, in small groups or larger groups, depending on the profile

of the autistic child or adolescent;

‒

implement them in routine activities, for example, during activities of daily living, sports, cultural
or leisure activities, and in natural settings;

‒  use video modelling to facilitate the learning of adaptive behaviours and daily living skills, where

appropriate for the autistic child or adolescent;

‒  develop training and protocols to integrate social skills groups into routine practice.

3.2.4.  Interventions focused on sensory processing and motor skills

Sensory and motor assessment is a key prerequisite for intervention (see GPG 2018).

This assessment includes [GPG 2012]:

‒  screening  for  sensory  impairments  as  for  any  child,  with  referral  to  specialist  medical

‒

‒

consultations where appropriate (ENT, ophthalmology);

identification of preferred sensory modalities;

identification  of  atypical  responses  to  sensory  experiences  (tactile,  proprioceptive,  auditory,
visual, gustatory or olfactory);

‒  monitoring the development of:

  gross motor skills (general dynamic coordination, balance, posture);



fine motor skills and visuomotor coordination, including graphomotor skills;

  muscle tone regulation;

  body awareness (body knowledge, laterality and imitation abilities);

  spatio-temporal organisation,  praxis and gnosis.

Sensory processing

Taking  sensory  functioning  into  account  is  essential  to  identify  the  specific  actions  and  adaptations
required to promote sensory comfort for each autistic child or adolescent. Sensory assessments enable
the identification not only of sensory processing difficulties in autistic children and adolescents but also
their sensory strengths and preferences, which can be built upon as potential competencies.

  Sensory assessment

It is recommended to:

‒  carry  out  standardised  sensory  assessments,  where  possible,  in  a  wide  range  of  contexts,
combining proxy assessment and direct assessment of the autistic child or adolescent, including
situational observations;

‒  analyse sensory aspects in terms of hyper- and/or hyposensitivity, as well as sensory seeking

or avoidance behaviours;

‒

regularly evaluate sensory-based strategies in order to measure their effects and make the nec-
essary adjustments.

  Sensory adaptations

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

30

It is recommended to:

‒  enable  autistic  children  or  adolescents  to  access  adapted  spaces  with  graded  sensory
modifications, or spaces allowing them to withdraw without compromising their participation;

‒

reduce sources of visual and auditory distraction in shared environments;

‒  use sensory protection strategies where needed;

‒

incorporate the specific sensory profile of the autistic child or adolescent into the personalised
plan so as to ensure its application in all environments and activities

Motor skills

It is recommended to:

‒  assess  motor,  praxis,  postural,  tone  or  gnosis-related  difficulties  that  may  negatively  affect
independence (hygiene, dressing, eating, leisure) and learning at school. A comprehensive as-
sessment of motor functioning is required (HAS GPG 2018);

‒  offer  psychomotor  therapy  and/or  occupational  therapy  and/or  physiotherapy  and  adapted
physical  activity,  sometimes  in  combination, to support  the  development  of motor and  praxis
skills;

‒  adapt  the  child’s  or  adolescent’s  sensorimotor  environment  to  avoid  overstimulation  or,  con-
versely,  provide appropriate levels of stimulation, particularly in terms of noise, light and tex-
tures.

  Early signs (0–2 years)

In  the  presence  of  very  early  atypical  developmental  signs  (e.g.  severe  hypotonia,  poor  postural
adjustment,  reduced  social  engagement),  it  is recommended  to  offer  standardised  assessment  and
early intervention in psychomotor therapy, physiotherapy or ***ergotherapy***.

In  the  presence  of  clear  neurological  signs,  atypical  postures  or  delayed  walking,  a  physiotherapy
assessment and concurrent intervention should be prescribed.

  From age 3 and during school years

It is recommended to:

‒

‒

include a physical or sporting recreational activity in the intervention programme;

identify, through standardised assessment, difficulties in coordination or organisation of gross
and fine motor skills;

‒  provide  task-oriented  motor  interventions,  individually  and/or  in  groups,  to  support  the

development of motor skills relevant to independence, learning and socialisation;

‒  adapt the physical and social environment to meet specific motor needs;

‒

raise parental awareness regarding environmental adaptations within the home.

3.3.  Environmental adaptations

The  aim  of  contextual  adaptations  is  to  enable  autistic  children  and  adolescents  to  become  active
agents in their environment while making it predictable and accessible.

3.3.1.  In the spatial environment

It is recommended to:

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

31

‒

take  account  of  the  specific  support  needs  of  each  autistic  child  or  adolescent  and  raise
awareness among all professionals, including those in public settings;

‒  provide a structured environment adapted to the needs of autistic children and adolescents;

‒  ensure  the  sensory  and  physical  comfort  of  the  autistic  child  or  adult  to  facilitate  mobility,

learning and activities;

‒  promote  the modularity of  living  spaces  to  enable  their  adaptation  to the  learning  and  social

participation needs of autistic children or adolescents;

‒  provide spaces in which autistic children or adolescents can relax;

‒  differentiate  the  functions  of  rooms  by  limiting  the  number  of  uses  per  space  (e.g.  clearly

separating activity and living spaces, ideally with one space reserved for each function);

‒  provide, within the habitual environment, spaces enabling the modulation of sensory input for

those who need it, while ensuring freedom of movement.

3.3.2.  Temporal organisation

It is recommended to:

‒  personalise autistic children’s and adolescents’ daily routines, adjusting the pace and intensity

of stimulation to prevent risks of over-occupation and/or under-occupation and fatigue;

‒  structure  each  autistic  child  or  adolescent’s  individual  timetable  while  maintaining  sufficient

flexibility to meet specific individual needs;

‒  clarify the duration and sequencing of activities.

3.3.3.  In terms of information

It is recommended to:

‒  present information, instructions and schedules in a clear and adapted manner (notably through

visual augmentative and alternative communication);

‒

involve  the  child  or  adolescent  in  planning  their  schedule  and  to  inform  them  of  changes  in
spaces, durations and sequences (before, during and after each stage);

‒  employ clear, concrete and unambiguous language adapted to the child’s or adolescent’s level
of  understanding  and,  where  necessary,  use  visual  supports  (e.g.  photo  sequences,
pictograms, objects, schedules) and avoid their premature withdrawal by gradually fading out
their use;

‒  consistently  use  the  child’s  or  adolescent’s  habitual  mode  and  tools  of  communication  in  all

situations.

3.3.4.  In terms of environmental adaptations

It is recommended to:

‒

‒

‒

raise awareness among all stakeholders, including those in public settings, regarding contextual
adaptations that facilitate the participation of autistic children and adolescents;

raise awareness among professionals in the built environment (architects, interior and outdoor
designers, maintenance and safety personnel) of the specific characteristics of autistic children
and adolescents (e.g. perceptions of time and space, sensory features);

take the specific needs of autistic people into account in the definition of universal design and
accessibility.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

32

3.4.  Technical aids

3.4.1.  Remote activities: approaches and monitoring14

It is recommended that:

‒

‒

in the absence of an appropriate alternative, and where relevant, professionals consider the use
of remote care for autistic children or adolescents together with their family;

the implementation of remote care be the result of a shared decision-making process between
the autistic child or adolescent, their family and the professional, with the latter providing clear,
fair and accessible information, and obtaining informed, formalised and documented consent
from the parents or legal guardian;

‒  professionals  delivering  remote  care  to  autistic  children  or  adolescents  assess

the
appropriateness of this approach, taking account of their specific needs as well as the material
and technical conditions;

‒  professionals  delivering  remote  care  to  autistic  children  or  adolescents  ensure  that  family
caregivers are able to use the required technologies, and where necessary shall direct them
towards, or provide, appropriate training or support.

It is recommended to:

‒

‒

regularly assess the continued appropriateness of remote care, including any potential loss of
opportunity;

refrain from using remote care in certain situations where the child’s or adolescent’s condition
requires in-person presence or where the material conditions are unsatisfactory;

‒  make sure that the implementation of remote care is adapted to the characteristics and needs
of  autistic  children  or  adolescents,  their  parents,  and  the  organisational  and  professional
constraints of those delivering the intervention

‒  provide,  on  the  one  hand,  a  wide  field  of  view  for  the  camera  in  order  to  capture  as  many
elements  of  the  environment  as  possible,  and  on  the  other  hand,  guarantee  the  effective
availability of the professional supporting the child or family during the session;15

‒  ensure  that  remote  interventions  follow  the  same  guidelines  as  those  for  face-to-face

interventions.

3.4.2.  Tele-expertise

It is recommended to facilitate access to tele-expertise from autism specialists by improving the visibility
of this provision at local and regional levels. This visibility notably enables primary care and medico-
social professionals to benefit from expert input supporting early identification, referral and follow-up of
autistic children and adolescents.

The  provision  of  tele-expertise  for  autistic  children  and  adolescents  and  their  families  should  be
specified and regularly updated throughout different regions nationwide.

14 Haute Autorité de santé – Telehealth – Les bonnes pratiques (HAS – Remote care – Best practices)
15 https://www.has-sante.fr/jcms/c_2971632/fr/teleconsultation-et-teleexpertise-guide-de-bonnes-pratiques

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

33

3.4.3.  Digital tools

As applies to the general paediatric population, general recommendations regarding screen use apply
to autistic children and adolescents.  The aim is to promote positive, appropriate and balanced use of
digital technologies.

Excessive  screen  use  reported  in  the  clinical  history  should  not  be  considered  a  cause  of  social
communication difficulties, nor should it delay the assessment of a possible autism spectrum condition
in the child.

When  used  in  a  structured  and  adapted  manner,  digital  technologies  may  serve  as  an  enabler  of
learning for some autistic children and adolescents and a support for their interests.

It  is  recommended  to  systematically  involve  autistic  children  or  adolescents,  their  families  and
professionals in the choice of digital tools.

It is recommended to provide information to facilitate their use and generalisation, taking account of
the functional profile of the autistic child or adolescent concerned.

3.4.4.  Research perspectives

Given the rapid development and market release of numerous technological tools – especially digital
ones – often without scientific evaluation, a high level of vigilance is required prior to their use.

It is recommended to:

‒

facilitate access to transparent information on available digital tools, including evidence of their
benefit, data protection considerations, and conditions of use and accessibility;

‒  promote  close  collaboration  between  healthcare  professionals  and  industry,  as  such

partnerships are essential to forge strong links between technical and clinical expertise;

‒  encourage  the  co-design  of  digital  tools  involving  professionals,  families  and  the  individuals

concerned;

‒  evaluate,  through  rigorous  interventional  research  using  appropriate  methodology  and
protocols, the clinical and organisational value of digital tools for use with autistic children and
adolescents.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

34

4.  Education, schooling and independence

Key messages

To  ensure  a  comprehensive  and  coherent  approach,  the  schooling  of  autistic  children  and
adolescents  requires  close  and  sustained  coordination  and  partnership  between  professionals
providing support or care and the parents.

Professionals  in  schools  and  apprentice-training  settings  should  receive  training  and  support
enabling them to adapt provision for autistic pupils and students.

Physical and sporting activities are an integral part of the intervention plan for autistic children and
adolescents.

Participation in leisure activities, holidays and cultural life should be supported by the autistic child’s
or  adolescent’s  broader  network  (family  and  professionals  involved  in  support  and  in  these
activities), taking account of their interests.

The schooling of autistic children and adolescents falls within the framework of the provisions of the
Law of 11 February 2005 on equal rights and opportunities, participation and citizenship for disabled
people.  These  provisions  aim  to  ensure  the  continuity  of  an  educational  pathway  adapted  to  each
pupil’s skills and needs. They prioritise mainstream schooling close to the family home.

It is recommended to inform the autistic child or adolescent, but also to involve them and seek their
participation  in  decisions  concerning  them  in  relation  to  their  support,16 both  at  key  stages  in  the
assessment,  planning  and  revision  of  their  personalised  plan,  and  on  an  ongoing  basis  in  the
implementation of the planned interventions [GPG 2012].

It is recommended to take account of the children’s or adolescents’ level of understanding and maturity,
as well as their preferences and interests [GPG 2012].

Listening to and informing the children or adolescents, while taking account of their views, should be
ensured at all times, within and between all teams involved in supporting them and their families [GPG
2012].

4.1.  Schooling

In  this  document,  the  term  schooling  refers  to  primary  school,  secondary  school,  further  education,
vocational training and university.

In accordance with the implementation of the Law of 11 February 2005, it is recommended to:

‒  ensure continuous schooling for autistic children and adolescents, without interruption, in order

to support learning and the development of social skills;

‒  ensure,  based  on  assessment  of  needs,  access  for  autistic  children  and  adolescents  to  all
educational provision (including human support) offered within the French education system (cf.
Figure 1);

decision-making (Art. L. 1111-4 of the Public Health Code).

‒  ensure regular  communication  between  families  and  professionals  regarding  the  educational

and learning needs of the autistic child or adolescent within their schooling;

‒  prevent risks of school bullying;

‒  develop  peer  support  roles  (pupils  or  students)  within  schools,  universities  and  vocational

‒  promote  schooling  within  the  local  environment,  close  to  the  family  home,  so  that  autistic

particularly into adulthood.

Schooling arrangements following a decision by the departmental disability centre

The personalised schooling plan (PPS), intended for pupils with disabilities, is developed with the
departmental disability centre and is binding on the national education system.

The  schooling  of  an  autistic  child  or  adolescent  may  require  an  official  decision  issued  by  the
departmental  disability  centre,  concerning:  localised  inclusive  education  units;  human  support:
teaching  assistants  for  pupils  with  special  educational  needs  (SEN);  institutions  and  services:
autism-specific primary teaching units, autism-specific nursery teaching units, special education and
home care services, specialised support and outreach service hubs; specialist educational institutes
for children with disabilities, teaching units, and outreach teaching units (cf. Figure 1).

It is recommended to:

‒  ensure continuity of human support for the autistic child or adolescent by limiting the number
of  different  SEN  teaching  assistants  involved  with  the  autistic  child  or  adolescent.  Where

changes of SEN teaching assistants occur, these should be clearly explained to the child or
adolescent;

‒  support  for  schools,  vocational  training  providers  and  universities  with  the  identification  of
autistic  pupils  and  assist  them  in  obtaining  diagnoses  and,  where  appropriate,  formal
recognition of disability by the departmental disability centres.

4.2.  Coordination and partnership on schooling for comprehensive

and coherent support

It is recommended to:

‒  optimise resources and avoid overlaps and fragmentation in support pathways;

‒  develop regular collaboration between families, school staff and other professionals (medical,
health and social care, independent practitioners) involved with autistic children or adolescents,
in order to ensure continuity of support throughout the school day;

‒  provide for the organisation of school catering services and out-of-school care within schools;

‒

involve school health services (doctor and nurse);

‒  anticipate admissions to autism-specific nursery teaching units with the various professionals
concerned  (coordination  and  referral  platform,  early  diagnostic  teams  and  departmental
disability centres) so that eligible children can be admitted in the year of their third birthday. It is
recommended  to  structure  and  ensure  the  transparency  of  admissions  to  autism-specific
nursery teaching units at territorial level;

‒  anticipate and secure, within autistic pupils’ educational pathways, their transitions from autism-
specific  nursery  teaching  units,  ***autism-specific  primary  teaching  units***  and  localised
inclusive education units

4.3.  Support and training for professionals in schools and vocational

training settings

It is recommended to:

‒  strengthen  and  expand  training  programmes  for professionals  by  including  teaching  on  child
development, the specific profiles of autistic children and adolescents, and learning strategies
and pedagogical responses adapted to them;

‒  strengthen  collaboration  and  coordination  with  independent  practitioners  (allied  health
professionals, psychologists, educators) and those in the health and social care sector working
with autistic children or adolescents, within schools, universities and vocational training centres;

‒  support  schools  and  vocational  training  institutions  with  the  implementation  of  good  practice

guidelines on autism;

‒  develop both initial and ongoing training on autism for teachers, school leaders, inspectors, SEN
teaching  assistants,  early  years  classroom  assistants,  and  other  staff  working  in  schools
(catering, extracurricular care, etc.);

‒  design  joint,  multi-professional  and  inter-institutional  training  programmes  bringing  together

professionals from the national education system and the medico-social sector;

‒  provide support for SEN teaching assistants to help them adjust their practices, in practice and
by  drawing  on  medico-social  resources  (e.g.  special  education  and  home  care  service,

specialised support and outreach service hubs, school-based self-regulation units, etc.) and/or
healthcare resources, and/or independent provision.

4.4.  Physical activity and sport, leisure, and culture

4.4.1.  Physical activity and sport

4.4.1.1.  Adapted physical activity

It is recommended to:

‒  develop adapted physical activity programmes that take account of the functional limitations,
interests,  skills  and  specific  needs  of  autistic  children  and  adolescents,  in  collaboration  with
multidisciplinary teams;

‒  offer  structured  and  organised  adapted  physical  activity  programmes  tailored  to  the  specific
functioning  of  autistic  children  and  adolescents,  using  appropriate  communication  tools  to
facilitate their understanding and participation;

‒

incorporate adapted physical activity programmes into the regular medical care of children and
adolescents with autism and into the support provided by multidisciplinary teams;

‒

regularly evaluate adapted physical activity programmes in order to adjust them accordingly.

4.4.1.2.  Physical activity and participation in sport

It is recommended to:

‒  systematically  incorporate  physical  activity  into  the  daily  lives  of  autistic  children  and
adolescents  and  their  families  in  order  to  improve  their  physical  health  (e.g.  weight  or  sleep
issues) and overall quality of life;

‒  systematically  include  physical  activity  in  intervention  programmes  delivered  by  educational,

healthcare and medico-social institutions;

‒

‒

inform  and  raise  awareness  among  families  of  the  importance  of  physical  activity  for  their
children, and provide them with resources and advice to facilitate access to these activities;

include modules on the benefits of physical activity in psychoeducation programmes for parents
and autistic children and adolescents;

‒  diversify the proposed physical activities, drawing on the strengths and interests of the autistic

child or adolescent;

‒  support  autistic  children  or  adolescents  and  their  families  to  encourage  their  involvement  in

physical and sporting activities;

‒  structure sporting environments and improve their accessibility, as with any other environment;

‒

regularly  assess  the  benefits  of  physical  activity  on  health,  physical,  behavioural  and  social
aspects;

‒  support autistic children or adolescents in their sporting practices in order to foster enjoyment

and develop relational and motor skills;

‒

regularly  assess  the  benefits  of  physical  activity  on  health,  physical,  behavioural  and  social
aspects;

‒  develop  specific  training  programmes  for  sports  professionals  so  that  they  can  provide

appropriate and adapted support for autistic children or adolescents;

‒  provide  training  for  healthcare,  health  and  social  care  and  independent  professionals  on  the

benefits of physical activity for autistic children and adolescents;

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

38

‒  use physical activity as a means of developing social skills and autonomy in autistic children

and adolescents.

4.4.2.  Access to leisure, holidays and culture

It is recommended to:

‒  provide material  and  human  support  to  leisure, holiday  and cultural  organisations  in  order  to

enable the participation of autistic children and adolescents;

‒  provide leisure and holiday facilitators and cultural venue staff with the information and tools

required to foster the effective participation of autistic children and adolescents;

‒  adapt  the  activities  on  offer  to  the  profile  of  the  autistic  child  or  adolescent  (communication,

cognitive, motor, sensory and emotional);

‒  adapt leisure, holiday and cultural settings to the sensory and communication characteristics of

autistic children or adolescents;

‒  use leisure, holiday and cultural activities to generalise the learning, communication and social

participation of autistic children and adolescents;

‒  ensure  consistency  of  support  by  developing  local  partnerships  between  educational,

healthcare or medico-social settings and leisure, holiday and cultural venues;

‒

involve and support families so that they can best prepare for their child’s participation in leisure
and cultural activities;

‒  develop  opportunities  for  exchange,  awareness-raising  and  training  on  autism  for  leisure

facilitators, holiday staff and cultural venue staff;

‒  develop  adapted  sessions  and  settings  to  enable  the  participation  of  autistic  children  and
adolescents,  and  facilitate  learning  and  generalisation  (visual  information,  attention  to  sound
and light, freedom of movement, quiet spaces).

In  the  absence  of  validated  evidence  for  animal-assisted,  music-based  or  art-based  mediation
techniques, these cannot be offered as therapies nor replace established interventions. However, they
may be offered to autistic children or adolescents according to their interests  and may contribute to
fostering their participation.

5.  Monitoring in primary and specialist care

Key messages

Autistic  children  and  adolescents  benefit  from  regular  medical  follow-up  in  primary  care  for
prevention and early management, with particular vigilance for comorbidities frequently associated
with autism (epilepsy, sleep, diet, digestion, etc.).

All healthcare professionals are made aware of autism, both in terms of approaches and adapting
care to the specific needs of the children or adolescents concerned, and in ways of supporting their
participation in care.

In the absence of any pharmacological or biomedical treatment specific to autism, any prescription
– of psychotropic medication in particular – must be strictly regulated, preceded by prior information
for families and an initial assessment, and accompanied by regular monitoring carried out in close
coordination with the autistic child or adolescent, their family, and the professionals involved in their
care.

Autistic infants, children and adolescents may also present physical or mental health conditions. These
conditions may or may not be related to their autism. Their identification may be all the more difficult
due to autism, particularly in terms of the perception and expression of symptoms and pain, and the
acceptance of medical procedures.

Health  monitoring  takes  account  of  conditions  associated  with  the  child’s  or  adolescent’s  autism,
including  other  neurodevelopmental  disorders,  epilepsy,  psychiatric  disorders  (particularly  during
adolescence), instinctual functions (diet, digestion, sleep), and behaviour.

5.1.  Physical and mental health monitoring

5.1.1.  Foundations of physical and mental health monitoring

It is recommended to:

‒

implement health prevention measures through regular medical consultations;

‒  carry out, as for any child or adolescent, systematic medical follow-up using the personal child
health record,17 which enables the collection and sharing of information with other healthcare
professionals and the family;

‒  ensure regular dental check-ups with a dentist and other specialists depending on associated

conditions;

‒  seek specialist advice through tele-expertise where appropriate;

‒  determine priorities for intervention on co-occurring conditions associated with ASD according

to their impact on the health and/or functioning of the autistic child or adolescent;

‒  carry out a specialist medical examination to define specific management arrangements in the

case of an associated condition, particularly psychiatric or neurological;

‒  systematically offer a genetics consultation as part of the aetiological assessment, in line with

current recommendations;

17 Le carnet de santé de l’enfant – Ministère du Travail, de la Santé, des Solidarités et des Familles

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

40

‒  provide  more  frequent  and  regular  medical  monitoring  in  the  case  of  prescribed  medication,
particularly psychotropics, in order to detect common adverse effects (e.g. extrapyramidal or
metabolic signs, changes in mood, appetite or sleep);

‒  conduct, without delay, a physical examination to investigate a medical cause in the event of

any unusual change in behaviour in the child or adolescent;

‒

repeat ENT and ophthalmological examinations, which may include a neurovisual assessment,
in the event of warning signs relating to hearing or vision, even if they were previously performed
at the time of initial diagnosis;

‒

follow the standard immunisation schedule for all infants, children and adolescents.

5.1.2.  With a view to health prevention

It is recommended to:

‒  encourage and promote regular physical activity to limit the effects of sedentary behaviour;

‒  provide health education by promoting good nutritional practices (such as a varied and balanced
diet) and daily hygiene (such as toothbrushing), in line with those recommended for any child
or adolescent of the same age;

‒  develop knowledge of pain and its identification, especially as some manifestations of pain may
be atypical and expressed through behaviours such as self- or hetero-aggression, or increased
withdrawal;

‒  pay particular attention to specific pain, including gynaecological pain such as menstrual pain;

‒

increase  the  use  of  pain  assessment  scales  that  are  standardised  and  adapted  to  the
communication mode of the autistic child or adolescent, such as the pain assessment grid for
individuals with intellectual disability (Grille d’évaluation de la douleur – déficience intellectuelle
– GED-DI) or the simplified pain assessment scale for non-communicating individuals (Échelle
simplifiée d’évaluation de la douleur chez les personnes dyscommunicantes – ESDDA);

‒  ensure appropriate therapeutic management of pain;

‒  ensure regular monitoring of sleep quality in order to detect and treat any sleep disorder;

‒  ensure regular monitoring of bowel function, with particular attention to the risk of constipation,

in order to anticipate and manage potential complications;

‒  carry  out  a  comprehensive  assessment  to  adapt  interventions  in  cases  of  food  selectivity,
intestinal  conditions  or  restrictive  diets,  including  an  evaluation  of  dental  health  or  any  other
factor increasing the risk of nutritional deficiency. Food selectivity, which is common in autistic
children  and  adolescents,  may  pose  a  health  risk  and  requires  appropriate  behavioural
management and dietary support;

‒  analyse any unusual change in behaviour in order to identify possible causes such as: inade-
quacies in environmental adaptations or support; pain-related manifestations; physical health
problems and/or psychiatric disorders. These observations lead to specific and coordinated re-
sponses involving both medical interventions and adjustments to support. (cf. 10).

5.1.3.  Focus: sleep disorders

It  is  recommended  to    screen  systematically  for  sleep  disorders,  which  are  common  in  autism
(particularly insomnia), by asking parents about the sleep habits of the autistic child or adolescent and,
where necessary, using specific tools such as sleep questionnaires and sleep diaries.

It  is  recommended  to  provide  families  with  information  about  behavioural  approaches  to  managing
sleep disorders that is adapted to the age and level of functioning of the autistic child or adolescent .

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

41

The  initial  management  of  sleep  disorders  is  based  on  sleep  hygiene,  for  both  the  autistic  child  or
adolescent  and  their  family.  This  includes  establishing  conditions  conducive  to  healthy  routines,
creating  a  sensory  environment  adapted  to  the  child’s  needs  (lighting,  temperature,  noise,  etc.),
implementing regular bedtime routines, and using behavioural therapies.

It is important to explore the impact of sleep disorders in the autistic infant, child or adolescent on the
family. As with any other intervention, it is important to take parents’ observations into account, involve
them in the strategies implemented, and consider long-term support for the entire family.

In cases of chronic sleep disorders, sudden onset or worsening of symptoms, it is recommended to
investigate possible causes, including medical causes (e.g. pain), comorbidities (e.g. ADHD, restless
legs syndrome, parasomnias, sleep apnoea, epilepsy), and, where necessary, to refer to a specialist
sleep clinic.

It is recommended to consider treatment with melatonin (immediate- or prolonged-release) in cases
where non-pharmacological interventions have only partial effectiveness and where sleep disorders
have a significant impact on daily life, always in combination with non-pharmacological measures (cf.
Figure 2) (see § 5.3.4 Prescription of melatonin).

It  is  recommended  to  regularly  reassess  the  effectiveness,  tolerance  and  relevance  of  melatonin
treatment within the overall care context.

5.2.  Preparation for consultations with healthcare professionals

5.2.1.  Domains of awareness regarding the specific features of autism

recommended for healthcare professionals

‒  Specific functional characteristics in autism:

‒

importance  of  taking  the  knowledge  and  observations  of  regular  caregivers  (parents  or
professionals) into  consideration  with  regard  to  the  specific  patterns  of functioning  of  autistic
children or adolescents;

‒  adaptation of the reception of autistic children or adolescents: reducing waiting times; allowing
for  longer  consultations;  adapting  environments;  enabling  gradual  familiarisation  with  care,
notably through “practice consultations” and “social stories”;

‒  systematic  identification  of  pain  using  standardised  scales  adapted  to  autism  (e.g.  pain
assessment  grid  for  individuals  with  intellectual  disability  (Grille  d’évaluation  de  la  douleur  –
déficience  intellectuelle  –  GED-DI)  or  the  simplified  pain  assessment  scale  for  non-
communicating  individuals  (Échelle  simplifiée  d’évaluation  de  la  douleur  chez  les  personnes
dyscommunicantes – ESDDA));

‒

recourse,  where  necessary, to  dedicated  support  services  for  healthcare  provision  to  people
with disabilities (such as Handiconsult, Handisoins, Handisanté, Handident) and to tools such
as SantéBD or Handiconnect.

5.2.2.  Recommended approach to ensure appropriate care and support

the active participation of the autistic child or adolescent and their
family

‒  Listening to and taking account of the family’s observations; encouraging shared observation
between  the  family  and  professionals  to  enable  early  identification  of  health  problems,
manifestations  of  pain  and  unusual  behavioural  changes,  and  emphasising  the  written
traceability of shared information;
