42

‒

involving  the  autistic  child  or  adolescent  and  addressing  them  directly,  and  implementing
gradual  familiarisation  with  routine  care,  particularly  medical  and  dental  care  (for  example,
practice consultations, educational workshops using medical equipment);

‒  using  appropriate  tools  to  prepare  for  care,  such  as  augmentative  and  alternative
communication (AAC) materials, and adapting the environment while taking account of autistic
children’s or adolescents’ specific patterns of functioning, notably the sensory, communication,
cognitive and motor aspects;

‒  basing  this  familiarisation  on  close  partnership  between  the  family  and  the  professionals

concerned;

‒

implementing  educational  actions  to  help  autistic  children  or  adolescents  better  understand,
name and identify parts of their body, thereby facilitating the identification and localisation of
pain.

5.2.3.  Recommended implementation of care during consultations

‒  Taking account of the autistic child’s or adolescent’s ability to manage waiting when organising

consultations;

‒

informing  healthcare  professionals,  in  advance  of  the  consultation,  about  the  need  to  adapt
reception and care for the autistic child or adolescent;

‒  consulting  the  usual  support  network  (family  and  professionals)  to  identify  strategies  that
facilitate the delivery of care and allowing family members or professionals to be present during
the consultation (ensuring the consent of the autistic child or adolescent);

‒  enabling the autistic child or adolescent to anticipate the delivery of care by preparing them and
explaining  the  different  stages  using  visual  supports  or  other  appropriate  tools,  and  by
progressively introducing medical equipment;

‒  managing pain and discomfort related to care by anticipating and adapting strategies according
to  the  response  patterns  of  autistic  children  or  adolescents,  using  non-pharmacological
approaches such as distraction and, where necessary, analgesic treatments (examples: topical
anaesthetic dressing and equimolar mixture of oxygen and nitrous oxide – EMONO);

‒  when  administering  care  during  which  the  safety  of  the  autistic  child  or  adolescent  is
compromised,  and  when  analgesic  and/or  sedative  pharmacological  options  and  habituation
methods are not feasible (or cannot be implemented), considering the possibility of using secure
temporary paediatric holding devices under their supervision and in the physical presence of a
doctor.  Their use is conditional upon prescription by a doctor and requires the informed consent
of the autistic child or adolescent and their parents, including the reasons for and modalities of
use.

5.3.  Medications and other biomedical interventions for co-occurring

conditions

Pharmacological  treatments,  and  more  generally  any  treatments,  examinations  and  medical
investigations that may be prescribed for autistic infants, children and adolescents must comply with
the principles of obtaining and respecting patient consent, as set out in the French Public Health Code
[GPG 2012].

Parents must receive clear and informed information about the expected benefits and possible risks of
the  various  investigations,  treatments  or  preventive  actions  (Article  L.1111-2  of  the  Public  Health
Code). In accordance with their rights (Article L. 1111-4 of the Public Health Code), they may oppose

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

43

the prescription of medication for their child, provided that such refusal does not entail serious risks to
the  child’s  health  (e.g.  life-threatening  situations,  self-injury  with  risk  of  severe  sequelae,  etc.).  For
example, the admission of an autistic child or adolescent to an institution cannot be conditional upon
the  use  of  psychotropic  medication.  In  cases  of  aggression  endangering  other  persons  within  the
institution,  solutions  must  be  sought  with  the  child  or  adolescent  and  their  family  to  ensure  the
protection of all [GPG 2012].

During  adolescence,  the  question  of  the  appropriateness  of  prescribing  contraceptives  should  be
considered [GPG 2012].

5.3.1.  General principles for pharmacological interventions in autism

spectrum disorder

In the absence, to date, of any curative pharmacological treatment for autism, medication prescriptions
(such as for psychotropic drugs) are symptomatic, for example to reduce the severity of behavioural
difficulties or to manage co-occurring conditions such as epilepsy,18 or ADHD.19

It is recommended to:

‒  use  pharmacological  prescriptions  within  a  multimodal  approach  combining  them  with

behavioural interventions and psychosocial support;

‒

favour monotherapy when prescribing psychotropic medication in order to limit drug interactions

‒  carry out a thorough prior assessment to justify any pharmacological prescription;

‒

take co-occurring conditions into account when prescribing.

5.3.2.  Information, monitoring and involvement of autistic children or

adolescents, their families and the professionals supporting them

It is recommended to:

‒  provide autistic children or adolescents and their families with information adapted to their needs
on  the  objectives  of  pharmacological treatment,  the  risks  of  adverse  effects  and  the  hygiene
and dietary rules to be followed to reduce these risks;

‒  obtain  parental  consent  (legal  guardians  or  tutor  where  applicable)  and  seek  the  informed

consent of autistic children and adolescents;

‒  ensure continuous collaboration between autistic children or adolescents, their families and the
professionals  supporting  them,  in  order  to  incorporate  their  feedback  and  the  collection  of
objective data into treatment monitoring, particularly to promote adherence;

‒  adapt  treatments  based  on  the  assessment  of  needs  and  the  views  of  autistic  children  or

adolescents and their family;

‒  provide the autistic child or adolescent and their family with precise information on the hygiene

and dietary rules to be followed when taking psychotropic medication;

‒  systematise  the  monitoring  of  treatment  efficacy  and  tolerability  within  shared  protocols

involving all stakeholders and families.

5.3.3.  Prescription and monitoring of psychotropic treatments

Practice surveys show that a high proportion of autistic children or adolescents receive psychotropic
treatments, even though most of the molecules used have not been granted marketing authorisation
(MA) for this indication or for this population [GPG 2012].

Under these circumstances, any prescription must be cautious, judicious and based on objective data
enabling the prescriber to regularly assess the benefit–risk balance for each patient [GPG 2012].

Other than under exceptional emergency situations, it is recommended that the initial prescription of
psychotropic medication be decided by a child and adolescent psychiatrist, psychiatrist, paediatrician,
paediatric neurologist or neurologist. The general practitioner is informed of the prescription and of its
modalities for renewal and monitoring [GPG 2012].

As  a  general  principle,  psychotropic  medications  should  be  prescribed  only  exceptionally  and  on  a
temporary basis in autistic children and adolescents. Regular reassessment of the indication (every six
months or earlier depending on the duration recommended by the MA) should be proposed, including
the implementation of a treatment break [GPG 2012].

Lack of efficacy or poor tolerance should lead to discontinuation [GPG 2012].

It is recommended:

‒  as a first-line approach and outside of urgent somatic situations, to prioritise recommended non-
the

interventions  before  considering

pharmacological,  psychosocial  and  behavioural
prescription of psychotropic treatment;

‒

in the event of any acute change in behaviour, systematically investigate an underlying medical
or  environmental  cause,  supported  by  a  functional  analysis,  before  prescribing  psychotropic
treatment (cf. Figure 3);

‒  before initiating any psychotropic treatment, to carry out a full physical assessment including
paraclinical investigations adapted to the clinical condition of the autistic child or adolescent and
to the monitoring requirements of the prescribed treatments;

‒

‒

‒

‒

to  initiate  psychotropic  treatments  at  low  doses  with  gradual  titration  to  the  effective  dose  in
order to monitor tolerance and efficacy;

to carry out regular evaluation, at each prescription renewal, of the response to psychotropic
treatment, including verification of the achievement of the therapeutic objectives set, adjustment
of dosage if necessary, and monitoring of clinical and paraclinical tolerance and adverse effects;

to  regularly  reassess  the  indication  for  psychotropic  treatment  in  order  to  avoid  unjustified
prolonged use, in particular through treatment breaks or deprescribing protocols;

to refrain from multiplying psychotropic prescriptions, ensuring rigorous coordination between
the various prescribing physicians;

‒

to avoid anticipatory prescriptions of psychotropic medication.

5.3.4.  Melatonin prescription

It is recommended:

‒

in  the  case  of  significant  and  chronic  sleep  disorders,  to  prescribe  melatonin  in  addition  to
educational, behavioural and hygiene and dietary measures (cf. Figure 2);

‒

to adapt the pharmaceutical formulation of melatonin to individual needs;

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

45

‒

‒

to standardise and secure the use of melatonin through clear initiation regimens and maximum
dose schedules;

in cases of sleep disorders improved by melatonin, to maintain melatonin prescription beyond
the age of 18 if chronic sleep disorders persist.

5.3.5.  Prescription of diets

Dietary regimens and food supplements have no specific indication in the treatment of autism.

Exclusion  diets  (for  example,  gluten-free  or  casein-free)  are  reserved  for  strict  medical  prescription
following  confirmation  of  a  diagnosis  of  food  intolerance  or  a  specific  gastrointestinal  condition  (for
example, coeliac disease). These diets require regular medical monitoring.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

46

6.  Adolescence and transition to adulthood

Key messages

The frequency of psychiatric comorbidities in autistic individuals from adolescence onwards requires
increased vigilance from professionals, in order to enable the earliest possible specialist intervention.

Continuity of care and appropriate interventions is ensured up to entry into adult life. By involving
the autistic adolescent or young adult and their family, professionals ensure coordinated transfer of
information and the establishment of necessary onward arrangements.

Initial  diagnosis  of  autism  during  adolescence  or  adulthood  is  of  critical  importance  in  ensuring
appropriate  care  and  support.  It  is  therefore  essential  to  prevent  any  risk  of  overdiagnosis  or
underdiagnosis  by  relying  on  a  rigorous  clinical  approach  that  is  both  multidimensional  and
multidisciplinary.

6.1.  Life course: continuity of care and appropriate interventions

It is recommended:

‒

‒

‒

‒

‒

‒

to anticipate transition to adult life from the age of 14-15 years;

to  develop  care  and  support  pathways  for  autistic  adolescents  and  young  adults  within  a
framework of self-determination and to support transitions in a coherent manner;

to  mobilise,  throughout  the  school  year,  medico-social  and  community-based  teams  and
schooling monitoring teams to undertake practical preparations for educational and vocational
transitions;

in order to ensure fluidity and coherence of the care pathway and in education (specialist  or
mainstream)  from  childhood  or  adolescence  to  adulthood,  that  the  team  responsible  for  the
child’s  or  adolescent’s  follow-up  should  provide  the  teams  responsible  for  ongoing  follow-up
with a written report on this pathway, with the agreement of the autistic child or adolescent;

to ensure continuity of care and specialised educational follow-up during transitions and over
time, notably the continued use of augmentative and alternative communication modalities;

to systematically establish early and coordinated collaboration with adult healthcare services at
the point of transition from adolescence to young adulthood (16–18 years).

6.2.  Risks of psychiatric disorders: prevention and monitoring

It is recommended to:

‒

identify,  during  adolescence  in  autistic  individuals,  warning  signs  of  depression  and  anxiety,
which  are  more  frequent  in  autism,  in  order  to  facilitate  referral  to  a  child  and  adolescent
psychiatrist or a general psychiatrist;

‒  develop  a  practical  guide  for  identifying  mental  health  problems  in  autistic  adolescents  and

young adults for primary care professionals, in order to facilitate detection;

‒  be  attentive  to the  increased  risks  of  stigmatisation  and  bullying  affecting  autistic  children  or

adolescents;

‒  directly explore the risk of suicidal ideation or suicide plans with autistic children or adolescents,
particularly those with co-occurring psychiatric conditions, gender incongruence and/or a history
of bullying, or physical or sexual abuse.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

47

6.3.  Late diagnosis

It  is  recommended to  facilitate  access  to a  diagnosis  of  autism  spectrum  disorder  at  any  age, as  it
enables  access  to  appropriate  interventions,  specific  rights,  and  contributes  to  better  self-
understanding for the individual concerned as well as improved understanding by those around them.

For an adolescent or young adult in whom autism is suspected, it is recommended, in conjunction with
their family, to discuss the value of a multidimensional diagnostic assessment.

It  is  recommended  to  develop  screening  and  diagnostic  tools  for  autism  spectrum  disorder  in
adolescents  and  young  adults  with  suspected  autism,  whether  or  not  an  associated  intellectual
disability has already been identified.

As initial diagnosis of autism in adolescence or young adulthood is of critical importance in ensuring
appropriate care and support, it is essential to prevent any risk of overdiagnosis or underdiagnosis by
adopting a rigorous clinical approach that is both multidimensional and multidisciplinary.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

48

7.  Autistic individuals with intensive needs –

profound autism20

Key message

Individuals with profound autism have specific needs that are intensive, continuous and general in
terms of support.

7.1.  Definition of the notion of autistic individuals with intensive

needs – profound autism

Autistic  children  and  adolescents  with  intensive  support  needs  –  profound  autism  –  are  those  who
require intensive and continuous support 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.

Intensive support needs – profound autism – should not be confused with severe behavioural disorders
(or challenging behaviours). The intensity of needs implies that they must be anticipated but does not
call into question either the diagnosis of autism, the need for early interventions, or the need for social
participation, access to education and access to all medico-social or healthcare services.

The intensity of support needs in these autistic children and adolescents becomes apparent over time
and not at the initial diagnosis, particularly when the child or adolescent does not respond sufficiently
well to early interventions implemented from the time of initial diagnosis and/or shows developmental
regression. The difficulties are likely to worsen in the absence of appropriate interventions. Autism with
intensive  support  needs  –  profound  autism  –  has  a  major  impact  in  terms  of  quality  of  life  and
psychosocial consequences for the child and their environment (family and caregivers).

Autistic  children  and  adolescents  with  intensive  support  needs  –  profound  autism  –  present  the
following characteristics:

‒  severe  intellectual  developmental  disorder,  resulting  in  significant  learning  difficulties  and  re-

quiring adapted educational approaches;

‒  significant  limitations  in  adaptive  functioning,  requiring  constant  supervision  to  meet  safety

needs and activities of daily living for the individual and their environment;

‒  absence  or  major  limitation  of  receptive  and  expressive  communication,  preventing  the
individual  from  effectively  understanding  their  environment  and  expectations,  and  from
effectively expressing their requests and needs.

It is recommended to:

‒  define the intensity of needs in order to determine the level of support required;

‒  anticipate the progression of these needs, which are likely to increase with age;

‒  plan enhanced support throughout the person’s life;

‒

implement  regular  medical  follow-up  and  continuous,  sustained  medico-social  and  social
support.

20 Profound autism, see Lord C, Charman T, Havdahl A, Carbone P, Anagnostou E, Boyd B, et al. The Lancet Commission on the
future of care and clinical research in autism. The Lancet 2022; 399: 271-334.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

49

7.2.  Principles of support for autistic individuals with intensive

needs – profound autism

It is recommended to:

‒  strengthen structuring of time, augmentative and alternative communication, and environmental

adaptations, particularly sensory adaptations;

‒

‒

increase staffing levels and material resources to enable the continuation of existing support
(medico-social, healthcare and educational) in order to avoid breaks in care pathways;

focus on maintaining acquired skills and developing autonomy in daily living (sleeping, eating,
washing, dressing, moving around, etc.);

‒  build on the interests and routines of autistic children or adolescents to engage them in socially

valued activities;

‒  ensure the safety of autistic children or adolescents in all environments;

‒  offer autistic children or adolescents and their families activities within the most inclusive setting

possible;

‒  enhance training and supervision for professionals;

‒  strengthen  human  support

resources,

including

respite,  support,  guidance  and

psychoeducation, in order to take account of parents’ and siblings’ needs;

‒

‒

‒

improve  preparation  for  the  transition  to  adulthood,  in  coordination  with  the  family  and  the
various adult support services;

identify and assess frequently associated conditions in children and adolescents with intensive
support needs  – profound autism – which may mask one another;

identify, through regular monitoring, somatic comorbidities (in particular neurological conditions
such as epilepsy) and psychiatric comorbidities, which are more frequent but also more difficult
to identify, as autistic children or adolescents with intensive support needs –profound autism –
rarely express their pain explicitly;

‒  make  use,  where  necessary,  of  solutions  developed  in  the  field  of  profound  and  multiple
disabilities, and to apply them to autistic children and adolescents with intensive support needs
(cf. HAS guidelines on profound and multiple disabilities).

7.3.  Points of vigilance for public health actions

It is recommended to:

‒  precisely identify individuals with autism with intensive support needs – profound autism – in

France in order to better plan responses to their needs;

‒  develop national information and training campaigns on autism with intensive support needs –
profound autism – so that its impact on the daily lives of individuals concerned and their families,
on professional practices, and on the development of specialised services is better recognised;

‒  develop  clinical  research  programmes  and  research  in  the  humanities  and  social  sciences

relating to this population.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

50

8.  Support for relational, emotional and

sexual life

Key message

Relational, emotional and sexual education21,22 should be adapted to the specific characteristics of
each autistic adolescent or young adult.

8.1.  For autistic children and adolescents:

It is recommended to:

‒  provide them with information adapted to their developmental age, their level of understanding
and their usual modes of communication, in order to support their expression – verbal and non-
verbal  –  concerning  bodily  changes  related  to  puberty.  The  information  provided  should  be
progressive,  concrete  and  supported,  where  necessary,  by  visual  materials,  pictograms  or
videos;

‒

teach them how to ask for help on these topics, by informing them of the existence of several
possible  contacts:  members  of  their  family,  support  professionals,  staff  from  family  planning
services or specialised resource centres (e.g. Intimagir);

‒  adapt existing educational materials to address the main themes relating to bodily and psycho-
affective development within relational, emotional and sexual education (in particular puberty,
menstruation, masturbation, emotional orientation and consent), taking account of the level of
understanding and the sensory and cognitive characteristics of the autistic child or adolescent.

In cases of gender incongruence or gender dysphoria in a person with autism spectrum disorder, a
cautious approach is required both in the diagnostic process and in the provision of support and care.
The complexity of these situations requires close collaboration between autism specialists and experts
in gender incongruence/dysphoria, in order to ensure a response adapted to the specific needs of the
individuals concerned. It is reiterated that there is no robust evidence regarding an association between
autism and gender incongruence/dysphoria.

8.2.  By the professionals supporting them, in collaboration with

families

It is recommended to:

‒

integrate,  on  a  regular  and  anticipatory  basis,  sessions  on  relational,  emotional  and  sexual
education  into  support  programmes  before  puberty,  and  then  throughout  adolescence  and
during  the  transition  to  adulthood.  These  sessions  are  aligned  with  national  education
frameworks while being adapted;

‒  adapt  relational,  emotional  and  sexual  education  content  and  tools  to  the  specific  profiles  of
autistic children or adolescents, taking account of their sensory, cognitive and communication
characteristics (e.g. social stories, social comics or visual digital tools, concrete objects);

21 A distinction is made between relational, emotional and sexual education, and
22 intimate, emotional and sexual life. Intimate, emotional and sexual life is a component of human dignity and one of the
fundamental freedoms.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

51

‒  place emphasis within these relational, emotional and sexual education tools on the concepts

of respect for self and others and explicit consent;

‒

raise awareness and provide training for all professionals working in social and medico-social
facilities or services, educational settings or healthcare institutions, as well as families, regarding
the importance of relational, emotional and sexual education, including the identification of signs
of vulnerability, maltreatment or abuse;

‒  offer autistic individuals who are victims of sexual violence adapted multidisciplinary support,
ensuring safe reception, respectful medical care and facilitated access to legal procedures, with
specific psychological support;

‒

incorporate  into  family  support  the  educational  approach  to  their  child’s  relational,  emotional
and sexual life.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

52

9.  Specific case of support within child

protection services

Key messages

Training of child protection professionals in autism is essential for the prevention of unjustified refer-
rals or safeguarding concerns, and for the provision of adapted support for the autistic children or
adolescents concerned.

Complementarity  between  the  different  fields  of  intervention  (child  protection,  justice,  education,
medico-social sector, etc.) is ensured through networked working methods involving stakeholders
as well as inter-institutional coordination meetings.

9.1.  Avoiding diagnostic errors and promoting an appropriate

pathway

It is recommended to distinguish between signs of autism and signs of proven maltreatment, in order
to avoid unjustified referrals or safeguarding concerns..

It is recommended to make the official list of medical experts in autism spectrum disorder, attention
deficit  hyperactivity  disorder  and  specific  learning  disorders  available  for  use  by  the  services
responsible for receiving and assessing safeguarding concerns (cellules de recueil des informations
préoccupantes) and judges.

It is recommended to promote close support for families whose autistic child or adolescent is subject
to a protection measure, in order to enable appropriate interventions.

For  any  autistic  child  or  adolescent  admitted  to  a  child  protection  service,  it  is  recommended  that
professionals ensure the provision of appropriate support and follow-up, and collaborate with specialist
and primary care services.

Prior to any placement decision concerning autistic children or adolescents, it is recommended that
child  protection  services  verify  that  the  placement  conditions  meet  the  individual’s  specific
characteristics and provide access to interventions that meet their needs.

It is recommended to plan a support pathway for the autistic child or adolescent, including an initial
assessment of their needs and the development of an individualised support plan.

9.2.  Training and support for child protection professionals and

foster families

It is recommended that child protection institutions and services comply with the HAS good practice
guidelines (GPG) as a prerequisite for any placement..

It  is  recommended  to  train  child  protection  professionals  to  develop  a  better  understanding  of  the
development  of  autistic  children  or  adolescents  by  generalising  an  initial  training  programme
throughout the child protection sector.

It is recommended to develop a disability resource team within child protection services that is trained
in evidence-based autism practices and able to intervene in institutions, at home, in residential care or
in foster families.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

53

It is recommended to provide specialist training for foster families, supplemented by parental guidance
and regular educational supervision, in accordance with current scientific knowledge.

It  is  recommended  to  promote  collaboration  with  parents  and/or foster  families  by  involving  them  in
diagnostic  and  follow-up  consultations,  in  order  to  implement  appropriate  guidance  within  the
framework of the protection measure.

9.3.  Adaptation of environments

It is recommended:

‒

‒

‒

‒

‒

‒

‒

‒

to  guarantee  an  appropriate  educational  environment  for  every  autistic  child  or  adolescent,
regardless of their care arrangements (within the birth family, the foster family or in a residential
care setting);

to anticipate and prepare for the removal of an autistic child or adolescent from the family home,
and for changes in their placement, in association with all medico-social, social, educational,
healthcare and, where necessary, emergency services;

to systematically support school professionals during a change of school placement so that they
are  able  to  provide  an  appropriate  welcome  for  the  autistic  child  or  adolescent.  This  work  is
based on cooperation between child protection services and all other stakeholders: the national
education system, the medico-social sector, healthcare services, and youth judicial protection
services;

to  ensure  that  changes  in  family  or  institutional  living  environments  for  autistic  children  and
adolescents do not interfere with the quality of the interventions required;

for autistic children or adolescents already supported within social and medico-social facilities
or services, to work in partnership with child protection services and foster families in order to
ensure consistency in support;

to  guarantee  that  interventions  for  autistic  children  or  adolescents  placed  under  the
responsibility of child protection services comply with current scientific knowledge and, for this
purpose, to train professionals in all child protection structures. Foster families must therefore
have access to parental guidance, caregiver training and the use of communication tools;

to develop the partnership between the justice system, child protection, medico-social services,
the education system and healthcare services:

to maintain  and  preserve  the  implementation  of recommendations  in  accordance  with  Action
Sheet  38  of  the  Autism  Plan-2017  and  the  proposals  of  the  2015  report  of  the  Defender  of
Rights.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

54

10. Prevention and responses to challenging

behaviours

Key message

The  management  of  challenging  behaviours  displayed  by  certain  autistic  children  or  adolescents
requires a medical assessment, a functional analysis and behavioural interventions.

For  the  prevention  and  management  of  challenging  behaviours,  refer  to  the  professional
good practice guideline “Les comportements-problèmes” [“Challenging Behaviours”] (sec-
tions 1 – prevention strategies, 2 – intervention strategies and 3 – calm withdrawal and sooth-
ing  spaces)  (HAS/former  ANESM),  23  in  addition  to  the  guide  entitled  “Qualité  de  vie :
handicap, les problèmes somatiques et les phénomènes douloureux” [“Quality of Life: Disa-
bility, Somatic Conditions and Painful Phenomena”].24

10.1. Challenging behaviours: prevention, support and management

For  every  autistic  child/adolescent,  every  personalised  plan,  whatever  the  setting  in  which  it  is
implemented,  must  include  actions  designed  to  prevent  and,  where  appropriate,  reduce  or  resolve
challenging behaviours [GPG 2012].

Among the interventions proposed to prevent the occurrence of challenging behaviours, the following
are recommended [GPG 2012]:

‒

implementation of a consistent augmentative and alternative communication system across the
different living environments of the child/adolescent when they have little or no spoken language
(Grade C);

‒  adaptation  of  the  environment  (e.g.  spatial  and  temporal  structuring,  sound  and  lighting

environment, etc.);

‒  anticipation of situations that usually trigger challenging behaviours.

Not every behavioural characteristic systematically requires a specific intervention designed to reduce
it [GPG 2012].

In the  event  of  behavioural  difficulties,  it  is recommended,  in  collaboration  with  the  parents  and the
child’s/adolescent’s usual support network, to investigate [GPG 2012]:

‒  somatic comorbidities or manifestations of pain, using an observational pain assessment scale;

‒

the contexts  in  which  challenging  behaviours  occur  and  their function,  in  order  to  determine,
through  functional  assessment,  the  factors  triggering,  maintaining  or  reinforcing  these
behaviours.

23 https://www.has-sante.fr/jcms/c_2834964/fr/les-comportements-problemes-au-sein-des-etablissements-et-services-accueillant-
des-enfants-et-adultes-handicapes
https://www.has-sante.fr/jcms/c_2833763/fr/les-espaces-de-calme-retrait-et-d-apaisement
24 “Qualité de vie : handicap, les problèmes somatiques et les phénomènes douloureux” Haute Autorité de Santé - Qualité de vie :
handicap, les problèmes somatiques et les phénomènes douloureux

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

55

In the event of behavioural difficulties requiring a specific educational intervention or pharmacological
treatment, these may be initiated in parallel with medical investigations for somatic causes, but must
not replace them [GPG 2012].

In  the  event  of  challenging  behaviours  (significant,  intense,  repeated  or  persistent  disturbance,  or
behaviour  presenting  danger  to  the  child/adolescent  or  to  their  environment  and  compromising
learning,  adaptation  and  social  inclusion),  it  is  recommended  to  promote  the  learning  of  adaptive
behaviours through appropriate psychological or educational techniques [GPG 2012].

Among the  interventions  proposed  to  encourage  the  learning  of  adaptive  behaviours  with  a  view to
reducing the frequency or intensity of challenging behaviours, the following are recommended [GPG
2012]:

‒  behavioural psychoeducational techniques (Grade C);

‒  any intervention achieving such learning through positive reinforcement of the child/adolescent;

‒  certain  pharmacological  treatments  (cf.  §  4.4),  in  association  with  the  non-pharmacological

strategies mentioned above.

In the event of self-injurious behaviour, the use of specific protective equipment may be considered
(such as a helmet) [GPG 2012].

10.2. Implementation of resolution strategies for challenging

behaviours and crises in order to avoid breakdowns in support

The  reduction  of  challenging  behaviours,  beyond  its  potential  impact  in  terms  of  improving  the
individual’s quality of life, enables the avoidance or at least the limitation of breakdowns in support and
subsequent inappropriate care pathways [GPG 2012].

It is recommended that professionals responsible for the follow-up of the child/adolescent [GPG 2012]:

‒

identify and assess the problematic nature of behaviours through consultation between parents,
their  child  and  professionals,  using  specific  tools.  Challenging  behaviours  require  broader
reflection on the support provided and the resulting way of life for the individual. This requires
observation, analysis of repeated situations leading to the behaviour, vigilance, knowledge of
alternative situations, and continuity within the educational and/or school team;

‒  bring together observations from the family and the various professionals involved (cf. crisis);

‒

identify  this  issue  within  the  institutional  project  and  implement  resources  to  enable  its
management;

‒  develop  tools  facilitating  the  identification  and  analysis  of  these  challenging  behaviours
(frequency,  circumstances,  events  or  interactions  favouring  or,  conversely,  stopping  the
behaviour; analysis of solutions already tested and those leading to positive outcomes), from
their onset, and establish specific alert procedures;

‒  disseminate internally the factors covered by identification procedures: personal, psychological

and somatic factors, family and institutional interactional factors, contextual factors;

‒

train professionals to manage these situations;

‒  prepare,  where  hospitalisation  is  unavoidable,  the  conditions  of  admission  with  the receiving
hospital, as well as the conditions for return to the child’s/adolescent’s usual living environment.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

56

11. Role and training of professionals

Key messages

The clinical practice guidelines on autism apply to all initial and ongoing training programmes, what-
ever the professions concerned.

When conducted in compliance with good practice guidelines, the supervision of professional prac-
tice is a key driver of continuing professional development, promoting both the appropriation and the
concrete implementation of these recommendations in everyday professional practice.

Professionals contribute to the quality of care pathways for autistic children and adolescents through
a multidisciplinary and coordinated approach.

For  care  pathways  and  coordination,  refer  to  the  professional  clinical  practice  guideline
entitled “Pratiques de coopération et de coordination du parcours de la personne en situation
de handicap” [Cooperation and Coordination Practices in the Care Pathway of Persons with
Disabilitites].25.

11.1. Training and supervision of professionals

The need to update professionals’ knowledge in the field of autism applies to all professionals working
with autistic children or adolescents, regardless of their mode of practice or sector of activity, but also
to professionals working within departmental disability centres, although the objectives and content of
the  training  provided  must  be  adapted  to  the  responsibilities  of  each  professional.  This  effort  must
begin during initial training and continue throughout professional life [GPG 2012].

It  is  recommended  that  all  members  of  the  relevant  teams,  including  managerial  staff,  benefit  from
these training plans, in order to promote consistency of support, facilitate and support any necessary
dynamics of change within the whole team, and avoid the isolated development of practices that could
disrupt the children and adolescents receiving support [GPG 2012].

Such  training  should  be  offered  regularly  and  supported  by  the  organisation,  and  subsequently
evaluated  with  regard  to  its  contribution  within  institutions  or  services  (improvement  in  functioning,
contribution to resolving potential difficulties, and the updating, where appropriate, of educational and
therapeutic techniques, etc.) [GPG 2012].

It is recommended to:

‒  develop the expertise of all professionals involved in interventions;

‒  encourage the sharing of practices and territorial collaborations in order to improve continuity

across care pathways;

‒  promote the training of all professionals involved in interventions;

‒  provide autism-specific training for primary care professionals (particularly general practitioners,
paediatricians, doctors and other health professionals working in PMI services and nurseries,
and professionals within follow-up networks for vulnerable newborn infants);

25 Haute Autorité de santé – Pratiques de coopération et de coordination du parcours de la personne en situation de handicap

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

57

‒

‒

improve  training  for  medical  and  non-medical  professionals  in  the  early  identification  of
developmental disorders;

incorporate scientifically validated knowledge on autism into the initial and ongoing training of
medical, paramedical, educational, social care professionals and psychologists;

‒  develop transdisciplinary and multiprofessional training programmes;

‒

incorporate  the  good  practice  guidelines  on  autism  into  the  initial  and  ongoing  training  of  all
professions involved in interventions for autistic children or adolescents and their families;

‒  establish a common core of up-to-date knowledge for all professionals involved;

‒  develop practical simulation-based training for the concrete implementation of recommended

interventions;

‒  enable families with recognised experiential expertise to participate in the training programmes;

‒  provide specific training for managerial professionals (heads of institutions or services, heads
of departments, etc.) regarding the impacts of supporting autistic children and adolescents on
recruitment, team management and departmental organisation;

‒

implement individual and team supervision, in accordance with clinical practice guidelines, on a
regular basis (according to the needs of professionals and autistic children or adolescents), in
addition to training, as a key tool for improving practice.

11.2. Role of professionals in care pathways and their coordination

Partnership with families

It is recommended to:

‒  develop parental guidance programmes at every stage of the pathway (identification, diagnosis

and interventions, transition to adulthood);

‒

incorporate  the  family’s  needs  into  the  overall  assessment  of  the  child’s  needs,  in  order  to
ensure comprehensive support;

‒  provide  families  with  clear  and  regular  information  regarding their rights,  available  resources

and possible interventions.

The personalised plan

It is recommended to ensure, on a daily basis, consistency in professional approaches between the
professionals involved (importance of stable reference points for individuals, consistency in the words
used to designate objects, consistency in routines and modes of functioning, as well as reference to
the institutional/service project, etc.) [GPG 2012].

It is recommended to organise the coherence and complementarity of the personalised intervention
plan  implemented  by  professionals  working  in  a  coordinated  manner  with  the  child/adolescent,
regardless of their sector of activity, with the life project of the child/adolescent and their parents and,
where the child/adolescent is recognised as disabled by the departmental disability centre, with the
personalised compensation plan26 and the personalised schooling plan27 [GPG 2012].

26 Articles L. 114-1-1, L. 146-8 and R. 146-29 French Code for social action and families.
27 Articles L. 112-2 and D. 351-5 of the French Education Code.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

58

Organisational arrangements for transdisciplinary work

The services of a wide range of professionals, institutions and agencies are required in order to adapt
the  support  and  follow-up  to  the  specific  needs  of  autistic  children  and  adolescents,  who  form  a
heterogeneous population [GPG 2012].

However,  the  involvement  of  multiple  professionals  and  settings  must  not  lead  to  fragmented
interventions. The key issue is to bring together the professionals required to work in a coordinated
manner with the child/adolescent, regardless of their sector of activity, from the outset of the process
of assessing the child’s/adolescent’s needs and resources, in order to ensure the complementarity and
coherence of interventions, the necessary adjustments to these interventions, and thereby secure the
care pathways while maintaining sufficient fluidity and flexibility [GPG 2012].

It  is  recommended  to  implement  a  transdisciplinary  approach  to  assessment  as  well  as  to  the
implementation and coordination of educational and therapeutic interventions, and to define in advance
the  operational  rules  governing  this  transdisciplinary  work  between  professionals  from  different
specialities within the same team or even from different institutions [GPG 2012].

These  operational  rules  must  be  known  and  shared  by  all  those  involved  with  the  child/adolescent
[GPG 2012].

These elements must also appear in the personalised compensation plan and, where appropriate, in
the personalised schooling plan [GPG 2012].

Organisation and coordination of pathways

It is recommended to:

‒  disseminate  within  each

territory

information  regarding

for
identification,  diagnosis  and  support  for  neurodevelopmental  disorders  (coordination  and
referral  platforms  for  neurodevelopmental  disorders,  early  childhood  health  and  social  care
centres, special education and home care services and other social and medico-social facilities,
autism resource centres, centres of excellence and specialist centres for language and learning
disorders,  Child  and  adolescent  mental  health  centre,  specialised  third-line  neuropaediatric,
child psychiatry or physical and rehabilitation medicine consultations);

the  graduated  pathways

‒  encourage local associations of healthcare professionals, in line with their healthcare pathway
organisation remit, to include pathways for autistic infants, children and adolescents among their
priorities;

‒  encourage territorial stakeholders to improve the fluidity of pathways for autistic children and
adolescents by formalising their modes of collaboration (coordination and referral platform, local
associations  of  healthcare  professionals,  independent  professionals,  follow-up  networks  for
vulnerable newborn infants, the national education system, social and medico-social facilities
or  services,  healthcare  services,  early  childhood  settings,  maternal  and  child  protection
services);

‒  ensure  effective  and  graduated  coordination  between  stakeholders  involved  in  identification,

diagnosis and intervention pathways;

‒

‒

identify a pathway coordinator responsible for monitoring and coordinating key stages. Pathway
coordination must be carried out by professionals competent in this field and trained in autism;

formalise  multiprofessional  discussion  times  for  autistic  children  or  adolescents  followed  up
exclusively in independent practice (with the identification of a coordinator) in order to monitor
the intervention plan and structure collaborations (cf. HAS recommendation on multidisciplinary
consultation meetings);

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

59

‒  build the pathway together with the family and the autistic child or adolescent, rather than merely

informing them after decisions have been taken;

‒  update  the  administrative  and  regulatory  frameworks  governing  authorisations  granted  to
medico-social  institutions  and  services,  in  order  to  adapt  them  to  the  specificities  of  autistic
people.

The coordination function

Within every institution, service or service provision arrangement, it is recommended to designate a
professional  or  professional  pair  responsible  for  coordinating  interventions  in  relation  to  the
implementation of the child’s/adolescent’s project [GPG 2012].

This coordination function may also be carried out by an independent practitioner.

The aim of this recommendation is to assist parents with the coordination of interventions concerning
their child and to avoid leaving parents isolated and solely responsible for a coordinating role they may
not have chosen to undertake. However, some parents may refuse this assistance and personally wish
to coordinate the interventions carried out in mainstream settings [GPG 2012].

The  professional  or  professional  pair  appointed  to  carry  out  this  coordination  function  for  the
personalised intervention plan and to oversee its implementation and monitoring [GPG 2012]:

‒  acts  as  the  main  point  of  contact  for  the  various  stakeholders  and,  in  this  capacity,
communicates  with  the  child/adolescent,  the  family,  team  members  and  any  other  person
concerned;

‒  ensures the smooth running of the different phases involved in developing and implementing

the personalised plan and the coherence of interventions;

‒  ensures, as a priority, the protection of the child’s/adolescent’s rights and interests.

It  is  recommended  that  independent  practitioners  liaise  with  the  other  professionals  supporting  the
child/adolescent concurrently with their intervention (and vice versa) [GPG 2012].

Information-sharing arrangements

A  coherent  personalised  plan  encompassing  various  forms  of  intervention  cannot  function  without
effective  coordination  and  continuous  interactions  between  professionals  within  the  framework  of
flexible and transversal communication both internally and externally [GPG 2012].

It is recommended to appoint a designated individual pathway coordinator on a long-term basis.

The  implementation  of  formalised  liaison  arrangements  between  stakeholders  (professionals  and
families) is recommended.

Situations or periods requiring heightened professional vigilance

Periods  or  situations  of  transition,  whether  related  to  the  child/adolescent  or  to  the  reception  and
support  arrangements,  are  recognised  as  creating  difficulties  for  the  child/adolescent,  professionals
and the family, and therefore require greater vigilance. As autistic people are highly sensitive to change,
it is recommended that professionals [GPG 2012]:

‒  pay  greater  attention  to  all  transitional  situations,  both  in  the  daily  life  of  autistic  children  or
adolescents  and  within  their  life  pathways,  whether  these  situations  are  linked  to  the
child/adolescent or to changes in support arrangements;

‒  exercise particular vigilance in the following situations:

  entry into adolescence,



transition to adulthood,

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

60

  changes in family circumstances or the child’s/adolescent’s immediate environment (death,
parental separation, departure of a sibling, change of individual special educational needs
support assistant, etc.),

  changes  in  intervention  arrangements  within  the  same  structure,  particularly  changes  of

group,

  change of schooling and/or support setting (first school enrolment, transition from nursery to
primary school, transition to lower secondary school, transition to upper secondary school,
admission to a medico-social institution, admission to residential accommodation for disabled
adults,  handover  between  two  intervention  teams,  particularly  between  healthcare  and
medico-social structures and vice versa, etc.),

  handover between diagnostic stakeholders and intervention stakeholders.

It is recommended [GPG 2012] to:

‒  share observations made individually by each professional (internally and externally), as well
as by parents, in order to promote collective vigilance (team meetings, oral and written feedback
to parents and professionals, etc.);

‒  address these  situations  with  the  participation  of  the  child/adolescent,  whose  preparation for

change and understanding of its coherence are essential;

‒  address these situations in collaboration with the parents

‒  ensure optimal preparation for transitions from one care setting to another (preliminary visits,
information-sharing, gradual integration prior to admission to the receiving structure, etc.);

‒

take account of possible future pathways for adolescents from the age of 16 years, and focus
learning activities and administrative or social procedures on the priorities of future adult life, in
order  to  facilitate  the  smoothest  possible  transition  to  mainstream  or  specialist  services  for
autistic adults;

‒  ensure the continuity of the support provided and of the tools selected, insofar as they remain
adapted to the individual’s needs, through the organisation of handovers between teams;

‒  strengthen support where necessary during these transitional situations.

Support for teams

It  is  recommended  to  organise  support  for  teams  through  collective  and  regular  reflective  practice
forums (once a month or once a quarter), facilitated by an external third party [GPG 2012].

It  is  recommended  to  avoid  professional  isolation  and  to  enable  professionals  to  work  under  the
guidance of peers, a manager or a supervisor [GPG 2012].

To prevent professional exhaustion and burnout, it is recommended to pay particular attention to team
support and to exercise heightened vigilance when a new professional takes up their post or when a
trainee is welcomed, as well as during sensitive periods involving difficult situations, particularly those
involving risks of violence or following violent incidents [GPG 2012].

Identification of reception and support services within a territory

It is recommended that every structure, regardless of its status or sector, clearly identify the approaches
proposed  and  the  specific  resources  made  available  to  children  and  adolescents  and  their  families
within the local area [GPG 2012].

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

61

Early access to interventions, rights and services

It is recommended to:

‒

implement early interventions, rehabilitation and access to rights without awaiting confirmation
of an autism diagnosis;

‒  use  all  available  resources  and  organisational  arrangements  compliant  with  good  practice

guidelines in order to facilitate early identification and diagnosis;

‒  organise territorial directories of identification, diagnostic and intervention services, and publish
them  on  the  websites  of  the  primary  health  insurance  funds,  autism  resource  centres,
coordination and referral platforms and departmental disability centres;

‒  encourage the use of tele-expertise in order to facilitate interventions and follow-up for autistic

children and adolescents.

11.3. Promoting clinical research

It is recommended to:

‒

involve experiential experts (autistic people, families and professionals concerned) in research
(participatory research);

‒  encourage  frontline  professionals,  families  and  children  to  participate  in  clinical  research

projects;

‒  continue evaluating the impact of recommended interventions on children’s pathways and dis-

seminating findings in order to support developments in professional practices.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

62

Glossary

Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC): AAC is a comprehensive approach address-
ing both receptive and expressive communication, with the aim of communicating differently (alterna-
tive communication) and more effectively (augmentative communication) than through usual or natural
means.

Challenging behaviours: “Culturally abnormal behaviour(s) of such an intensity, frequency or duration
that the physical safety of the person or others is likely to be placed in serious jeopardy, or behaviour
which  is  likely  to  seriously  limit  use  of,  or  result  in  the  person  being  denied  access  to,  ordinary
community facilities” (Emerson, 1995, 2001).

Respite schemes: a respite solution is:

‒  a means of responding to the needs of carers in order to relieve them within the current care-

giving context;

‒  a means of preventing any deterioration in the situation;

‒  a set of flexible, evolving arrangements and services adapted to the specific circumstances of
each carer. They may be occasional or regular, short term or long term, and may take various
forms.

Therapeutic patient education (TPE): TPE aims to help patients acquire or maintain the skills they
need to manage their lives as effectively as possible with a chronic condition. It forms an integral and
permanent  part  of  patient  care.  It  includes  organised  activities,  including  psychosocial  support,  de-
signed to make patients aware of and informed about their illness, care, healthcare organisation and
procedures, and health- and illness-related behaviours. The purpose is to help them (as well as their
families) understand their condition and treatment, collaborate and assume responsibility for their own
care, with the aim of helping them maintain and improve their quality of life.

Assessment of functioning (also referred to as functional assessment) and functional analysis
are two types of assessment with distinct objectives:

‒  assessment of functioning recommended by HAS (2018), also commonly referred to as multi-
dimensional functional assessment, aims to provide a cross-sectional description of a person’s
abilities and limitations in adaptive domains (autonomy, communication, social interactions, mo-
tor skills, etc.), in relation to their living environments. This approach is grounded in internation-
ally  recognised  bio-psycho-social  models,  and  supports  medico-social  and  educational
guidance and decision-making (ICF-CY, ICD-11, DSM-5);

‒

functional  analysis,  is  a  term  used  worldwide  (particularly  in  the  ABA,  ESDM,  TEACCH  or
SCERTS approaches) within an intervention framework. It aims to analyse how the person uses
their skills in different environments (family, school, work) in order to define individualised and
measurable objectives. It is often dynamic and context-dependent, and supports the implemen-
tation of educational, therapeutic or inclusion plans. Functional analysis also corresponds to an
interactive model linking challenging behaviours to the patient’s cognitions and emotions within
a given situation, together with their antecedents, on the one hand, and their consequences, on
the other.

Although some tools are shared (e.g. Vineland, ABAS), their use differs according to purpose (overall
functional assessment versus fine adjustment of intervention strategies).

Parental guidance: in a natural setting, this involves giving parents a clear explanation of the educa-
tional strategies to adopt, demonstrating them and enabling parents to practise them, while providing
constructive  feedback  to  help  parents  appropriate  and  generalise  them  in  everyday  life.  This  may

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

63

involve home visits, video feedback, tutorials, etc. (French Interministerial Delegation for Neurodevel-
opmental Disorders).

Psychoeducation: psychoeducation is an educational and informational approach targeting people
affected by a particular condition who require support to strengthen their adaptive capacities, by provid-
ing essential knowledge, improving skills, increasing social support and reducing feelings of isolation.

It may be directed towards several groups: children, adolescents, parents and relatives.

Supervision: supervision of professional practice is a continuing professional development arrange-
ment  enabling  professionals  to  apply  the  knowledge  acquired  during  training  to  concrete  everyday
situations. It is based on critical processes (observation, analysis, judgement, intervention) aimed at
improving the quality of support provided. It promotes coherence between frameworks, practices and
contexts. Preferably conducted with an external third party trained in the relevant methods and tech-
niques, it supports, for example, interventions with autistic children and adolescents, the appropriation
of assessment tools, learning strategies and guidance techniques. Supervision is adapted regardless
of the professional’s mode of practice (in the person’s home or within an institution).

Robust AAC systems: robust systems make it possible to communicate everywhere and at all times,
thereby enabling the expression of all kinds of messages corresponding to the person’s current and
future needs. They include a broad vocabulary incorporating different grammatical forms and enabling
grammatical development, organised in a coherent and stable manner, allowing for the personalisation
of  messages  and  use  by  the  communication  partner  (and  therefore  also  receptive  communication).
They  are  distinguished  from  basic  AAC  systems,  which  respond  to  a  current  need  and  enable  the
expression of a limited number of communication functions and messages.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

Annexe 1.  Questions identified during the scoping phase

The topics addressed in the 2012 Haute Autorité de Santé/ANESM guideline remain relevant. How-
ever,  the  recommendations  will  need  to  be  strengthened,  firstly,  by  the  current  state  of  scientific
knowledge in 2023 and, secondly, by the shared analysis of experts regarding the resulting practices.

In addition, certain themes will need to be explored in greater detail in light of the issues encountered
in practice. The following questions therefore need to be addressed.

  Assessments

How can the various assessments (for diagnostic purposes and for the assessment of functioning) be
better coordinated, and how can this lead to the definition of a comprehensive support pathway involv-
ing the various existing stakeholders, particularly within the framework of new partnership-based work-
ing arrangements (platforms, hubs, groupings, networks, bundled funding schemes, resource centres,
outreach teams, etc.)? How can pain identification and assessment, in particular, be better addressed?

  Interventions

 What clinical markers/indications can guide the adaptation of interventions to individual situations?
How should associated conditions (including other neurodevelopmental disorders such as intel-
lectual development disorder (IDD) and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), differing lev-
els of overall development (including high intellectual potential), and age be taken into account?
Particular attention should be paid to adolescence, a period conducive to the emergence of associ-
ated psychiatric disorders, psychological distress linked to increased difficulties in peer interaction,
as well as issues relating to emotional and sexual life (puberty, attraction, romantic relationships
and first sexual experiences, etc.) and gender (gender dysphoria).

 Which new intervention programmes or emerging therapies have been scientifically evaluated for
effectiveness and safety to a degree providing sufficient evidence to support their recommenda-
tion?

 Which models of care and support should be provided for forms of autism spectrum disorder asso-

ciated with severe challenging behaviours?

  The role of the family and carers

 How can family expertise be better incorporated, both in assessment and in the implementation of
comprehensive support, and how can parenting support be provided, particularly through “thera-
peutic education”, “parental guidance”, “co-intervention in rehabilitation workshops”, and “carer
training” initiatives?

 How should interventions be adapted in the presence of specific family vulnerabilities (psychologi-

cal trauma, language barriers, insecure housing, cultural barriers, financial difficulties, etc.)?
 How can greater account be taken of the specific timing and dynamics of each family in defining

and implementing the intervention programme for children with ASD? How can the support
provided to relatives be mobilised and adjusted according to the progression and key events
marking the family history and life course of the child with ASD (diagnostic process, orientation
decisions, developmental trajectory of the child, changes in family composition, changes in parental
availability and involvement of other family members, etc.)?

 What support should be offered to parents and siblings within a caregiver-support framework? How
can risks of caregiver exhaustion be identified? What respite solutions should be offered, particu-
larly in situations involving severe behaviours that challenge or crisis situations?

Beyond the further exploration of themes already addressed in the 2012 guideline, new issues have
emerged and/or raised questions among professionals, therefore requiring specific analysis.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

66

  Digital tools

 What types of technologies/computer functionalities are used to support learning (including school
learning), skills development (in communication, social interaction, etc.) and autonomy in children
or adolescents with ASD (37)? How relevant is the integration of these technologies into practice?28

 In what contexts can digital telehealth tools – notably teleconsultation, tele-expertise and telecare,
which developed considerably during the health crisis – be used with children primarily character-
ised by communication and social interaction difficulties? How can they be used for professional
training? What are the indications for their use with parents or with mainstream community part-
ners?

  Consideration of autism spectrum disorders within child protection services

Children recognised as disabled by departmental disability centres and supported by child protection
services do not always receive the care and support they require.(38)

 How can the consideration of possible autism spectrum disorders be improved in child safeguard-
ing reports concerning children at risk of harm? What specific interventions should be provided for
children with ASD receiving support within the child protection system? What forms of collaboration
should be established with child protection and judicial services?

  Inclusive social activities

As with any disability situation, the aim is to provide social activities that contribute to the child’s devel-
opment, promote varied social interactions within their living environments, and prepare them for adult
life.

 How can access to and participation in sporting, cultural, leisure and civic activities for people with

ASD be promoted within mainstream local facilities and services?

  Self-determination

“Having  the  power  to  make  decisions  for  oneself  is  a  learning  process  that  develops  throughout  a
person’s life.  Self-determination is an essential driver of identity construction for each of us and gives
meaning to the concept of full citizenship.”(32)

 How can comprehensive support be provided that not only enables children and adolescents, as

far as possible, to carry out the various activities expected of a person of the same age without as-
sistance from others, but also develops their ability to make decisions for themselves and take
charge of their own lives? How can greater consideration of the person’s self-determination and
experiential knowledge be given in the definition and implementation of support arrangements?

  Schooling

For minors and young adults, school learning and vocational training play a central role in their care
and support pathway. Between three and sixteen years of age, minors with ASD are necessarily en-
rolled in an educational pathway and encouraged to adopt the role of pupil. Over the past ten years,
schools  have  undergone  profound  changes,  notably  reflected  in  the  creation  of  new  arrangements
serving an increasingly inclusive education system. Whereas schooling was addressed in a short chap-
ter of the 2012 HAS guideline, educational pathways are intended, in the present guideline, to become
a central and cross-cutting component of the comprehensive support provided to children, adolescents
and young adults with ASD.

28 It should be noted that the Haute Autorité de Santé will not undertake any technological assessment as part of this guideline
update. On the basis of the existing literature and expert discussions, the aim is to indicate the level of evidence supporting the
usefulness of these technologies. Gaps in knowledge will also be examined.

HAS • Autism Spectrum Disorder: interventions and life pathways for infants, children and adolescents • January 2026

67

 How do care and interventions integrate into educational and vocational pathways, support the
child’s academic success and foster their fulfilment within the educational community, including
alongside other pupils and students29 (from nursery school through to higher education)?

  The life pathway

 How can the continuity and consistency of actions undertaken by the various stakeholders through-
out the life pathway of children and adolescents with ASD be ensured, particularly in preparing the
transition to adulthood?

29 Article L. 111-3 of the French Education Code: “Within each primary school [école], lower secondary school  [collège] or upper
secondary school [lycée], the educational community brings together pupils and all those who, within the educational establishment
or in connection with it, contribute to the fulfilment of its missions. It includes school staff, parents of pupils, local authorities,
educational associations supporting public education, as well as institutional, economic and social stakeholders associated with the
public education service. Within the framework of an inclusive school system, its cohesion is founded on the complementarity of
expertise.”
